title: Capability Advertisement as a Market for Lemons: A Trust Layer for Heterogeneous Agent Networks
summary:
Large language model (LLM) agents have begun to delegate work to one another. Protocols such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and the Agent2Agent protocol (A2A) let an agent publish what it can do and let others call it, and public registries of such agents are already appearing. These protocols assume an advertised capability is a static, truthful fact. A real agent is none of these things: its competence is probabilistic, varies with input, drifts when the underlying model is updated, and, because the agent is itself a language model, it can describe itself with complete confidence and be wrong. A caller therefore sees what an agent claims to do, not what it can do, with no principled way to tell a reliable provider from a fluent impostor.
  We argue these difficulties share one cause: the market for lemons. When quality is hidden and claims are cheap, good and bad providers become indistinguishable, honest reliability goes unrewarded, and the market decays toward its worst participants. Economics offers three remedies, signaling, screening, and reputation, and none are present in today's agent protocols.
  We make four contributions: (1) a failure taxonomy that names confident-wrong as a non-adversarial, correlated subclass of Byzantine faults that classical fault-tolerance mismodels; (2) a market-for-lemons model showing that faith-based protocols admit only a low-trust equilibrium; (3) the Trust Layer, a thin, protocol-agnostic narrow waist above MCP and A2A that adds probabilistic capability descriptors, screening, and reputation, and admits a separating equilibrium when the cost of sustaining an overclaim exceeds the gain from it; and (4) a reliability-composition bound for delegation chains with an end-to-end placement argument. The design needs no model retraining and degrades gracefully when its trust anchors are absent or corrupt.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a "market for lemons" problem in LLM agent delegation protocols (e.g., MCP, A2A), where agents' self-advertised capabilities are unreliable, and proposes a "Trust Layer" — a protocol-agnostic middleware that adds probabilistic capability descriptors, screening, and reputation to enable a high-trust separating equilibrium without requiring model retraining.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agent delegation protocols (MCP, A2A) treat advertised capabilities as static and truthful, but real agents have probabilistic competence that varies with input and drifts over model updates. Agents can confidently describe themselves incorrectly ("confident-wrong"), making it impossible for callers to distinguish reliable providers from fluent impostors. This creates a market-for-lemons problem where quality is hidden, claims are cheap, and honest reliability goes unrewarded.
AI.method: The paper makes four contributions: (1) a failure taxonomy classifying "confident-wrong" as a non-adversarial, correlated subclass of Byzantine faults; (2) a market-for-lemons economic model proving that faith-based protocols converge to a low-trust equilibrium; (3) the Trust Layer — a thin middleware above MCP/A2A incorporating probabilistic capability descriptors, screening, and reputation mechanisms that achieves a separating equilibrium when overclaiming costs exceed gains; and (4) a reliability-composition bound for delegation chains with end-to-end placement arguments. The design requires no model retraining and degrades gracefully when trust anchors are absent or corrupt.
AI.result: The analysis shows that current protocols admit only a low-trust equilibrium under the market-for-lemons model. The proposed Trust Layer can admit a separating equilibrium (distinguishing reliable from unreliable agents) when the cost of sustaining an overclaim exceeds the gain from it. The reliability-composition bound provides theoretical guarantees for delegation chains. The system works without retraining and degrades gracefully under trust anchor corruption or absence.
AI.conclusion: The fundamental problem in LLM agent delegation is not technical but economic — a market-for-lemons dynamic. Classical fault-tolerance models mismodel the "confident-wrong" failure mode. A lightweight, protocol-agnostic Trust Layer with probabilistic capability descriptors, screening, and reputation can resolve this by creating economic incentives that separate reliable agents from impostors, without requiring changes to underlying models.

title: Too Much of a Good Thing: When sim2real Efforts Impede Policy Learning (And What to Do About It)
summary: While sim2real efforts are necessary for effective policy transfer to hardware, there is such a thing as too much of a good thing. We argue that sim2real efforts have led to misaligned incentives with policy learning, resulting in simulator lock in and poor policy exploration due to the unreasonable constraints imposed by the real world. We offer a diagnosis and explanation of the current status of the problem, and propose a potential solution via a sim2sim2real paradigm that leverages the robot's kinematics as the sole design constraint.

AI.tldr: Excessive sim2real efforts create misaligned incentives, causing simulator lock-in and poor exploration due to real-world constraints. The authors propose a sim2sim2real paradigm where robot kinematics is the sole design constraint.
AI.motivation: Sim2real efforts are essential for policy transfer to hardware, but overemphasis on this process has created misaligned incentives. This leads to simulator lock-in and poor policy exploration because the real-world imposes unreasonable constraints that conflict with optimal learning.
AI.method: The authors propose a sim2sim2real paradigm that leverages the robot's kinematics as the sole design constraint, creating a more flexible and less constrained learning environment.
AI.result: By using kinematics as the sole constraint, the proposed approach aims to overcome simulator lock-in and enable more effective policy exploration.
AI.conclusion: A sim2sim2real framework that constrains only by kinematics offers a promising solution to the misaligned incentives and exploration challenges currently plaguing sim2real approaches.

title: Fewer, Better Frames: A Compute-Normalized Proof of Concept for Coherence-First World-Model Rendering with Model-Guided FSR4 Frame Generation
comment: 19 pages, 8 figures, independent systems proof of concept
summary: World models are often evaluated by native frame cadence, but higher nominal frame rate can trade away long-horizon scene stability. This article reports an independent proof of concept implemented using Overworld's Waypoint-1.5 family and WorldEngine runtime on a Windows fallback stack with ONNX Runtime + DirectML and an FSR4 DX12 bridge. The tested coherence-first branch generates higher-context anchor frames at a 15 FPS presentation-timeline cadence and reconstructs presentation to 30 FPS using latent-delta motion guidance and synthesized depth. It is compared against a lower-context cadence-first baseline that generates about 30 FPS natively under the same seed, route, control script, target presentation duration, and local time-scaling regime. Across forest, sword, desert, and snow scenes, the coherence-first branch preserves path geometry, object identity, large silhouettes, and depth layering longer, while the baseline degrades earlier into brightness drift and geometric distortion. Lightweight temporal metrics and paired videos support the visual comparison, with LPIPS favoring the coherence-first branch across all tested scenes. Here compute-normalized means approximately matched same-GPU, same-timescale operating points, not exact FLOP parity or measured realtime throughput. A separate heavier sword-scene probe suggests local non-monotonicity: more context and denoising did not automatically improve quality. These results support coherence-first allocation as a practical proof-of-concept strategy under limited inference budget, not as a finished realtime renderer.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates a proof-of-concept approach for world models that prioritizes scene coherence over native frame rate. Using Overworld's Waypoint-1.5 with WorldEngine runtime, a coherence-first branch generates context-rich anchor frames at 15 FPS and reconstructs to 30 FPS using latent-delta motion guidance, showing superior preservation of geometry and object identity compared to a higher frame rate baseline across forest, desert, and snow scenes.
AI.motivation: World models are often evaluated by native frame cadence, but higher nominal frame rates can sacrifice long-horizon scene stability. The authors seek to explore whether prioritizing coherence over raw frame rate produces better results.
AI.method: The coherence-first branch uses Overworld's Waypoint-1.5 family and WorldEngine runtime on Windows with ONNX Runtime + DirectML and an FSR4 DX12 bridge. It generates higher-context anchor frames at 15 FPS presentation-timeline cadence and reconstructs to 30 FPS using latent-delta motion guidance and synthesized depth. This is compared against a lower-context cadence-first baseline that generates ~30 FPS natively under identical conditions.
AI.result: Across forest, sword, desert, and snow scenes, the coherence-first branch preserves path geometry, object identity, large silhouettes, and depth layering longer than the baseline, which degrades into brightness drift and geometric distortion. LPIPS metrics favor the coherence-first branch across all scenes. A heavier sword-scene probe reveals non-monotonicity: more context and denoising did not automatically improve quality.
AI.conclusion: These results support coherence-first allocation as a practical proof-of-concept strategy under limited inference budgets, though not as a finished realtime renderer. The approach demonstrates that prioritizing coherence can outperform higher frame rate approaches for maintaining scene stability over long horizons.

title: MeDxAgent: Multi-Agent Consultation for Interactive Medical Diagnosis
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for health-related decision support. Yet most evaluations treat diagnosis as a single-shot task with complete information provided upfront, often as a multiple-choice selection. This diverges from clinical practice, where diagnosis is interactive and open-ended, involving sequential hypothesis refinement through targeted questioning. We address this gap. We build MeDxBench, a large-scale benchmark of 4,421 clinical cases across 20 specialties. We further propose MeDxAgent, a multi-agent consultation system for interactive diagnosis, and systematically study its prompt-, flow- and agent-level design choices. MeDxAgent achieves a 10.3% accuracy gain over the baseline on MeDxBench, closing 52.3% of the gap to a full-information oracle. We find that specific design choices: collecting demographics first, passing summarized dialogue for diagnosis, and feeding candidate diagnoses for targeted questioning, improve accuracy, mirroring how physicians reason, though their effect emerges fully only in combination. Code and dataset will be released upon publication.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce MeDxBench, a large-scale benchmark of 4,421 clinical cases for interactive diagnosis, and propose MeDxAgent, a multi-agent consultation system that achieves a 10.3% accuracy improvement over the baseline by emulating physician-like reasoning patterns.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLMs for health-related decision support treat diagnosis as a single-shot, multiple-choice task with complete information provided upfront. This diverges significantly from real clinical practice, where diagnosis is interactive, open-ended, and involves sequential hypothesis refinement through targeted questioning. The authors aim to bridge this evaluation gap.
AI.method: The authors construct MeDxBench, a large-scale benchmark comprising 4,421 clinical cases across 20 specialties designed for interactive diagnosis. They then propose MeDxAgent, a multi-agent consultation system, and systematically study its design choices at three levels: prompt-level, flow-level, and agent-level. Key design strategies include collecting demographics first, passing summarized dialogue history for diagnosis, and feeding candidate diagnoses to guide targeted questioning.
AI.result: MeDxAgent achieves a 10.3% accuracy gain over the baseline on MeDxBench, closing 52.3% of the performance gap to a full-information oracle. The study finds that individual design choices (demographics-first collection, summarized dialogue passing, candidate-diagnosis-guided questioning) mirror physician reasoning but their full benefit emerges only when combined.
AI.conclusion: Interactive, multi-agent diagnosis systems that incorporate physician-like reasoning patterns (e.g., demographics-first, summarized context, candidate-guided questioning) can substantially improve LLM-based diagnostic accuracy over single-shot approaches. The benchmark and agent framework demonstrate that closing the gap between LLM evaluation and real clinical practice is feasible, with code and dataset to be released.

title: CARVE: Certified Affordable Repair of Vetoed Maneuvers via Envelopes for Interactive Driving
summary: Interactive driving exposes a failure mode that is easy to miss in rule-aware autonomous-driving stacks: a hard-rule margin can be negative for an ego candidate even though a small lawful accommodation by a non-priority agent would restore feasibility. Existing rulebooks, shields, and reachability filters are strong at vetoing unsafe actions, while prediction-based planners model likely responses. Neither returns a runtime proof object that states which bounded multi-agent edit repairs the maneuver, who owns the edit, whether the request is right-of-way affordable, and what ego fallback remains if the request is not observed. We formulate this missing object as *interactive repair certification* and introduce *CARVE*, a prediction-free certificate layer over a finite lattice of ego-owned and agent-owned tactical operators. Agent-owned requests are admissible only inside \(B_j(s) = β(π_j)α_j^{\max}(s)\), a cooperation envelope that separates kinematic reachability from normative priority. The resulting certificate records the binding rule, repair category, repair set, responsibility-weighted cost split, and fallback. On 589 Lanelet2-geometry-grounded INTERACTION replay episodes, CARVE-Greedy accepts 98.64% of initially vetoed maneuvers and recovers 370/378 human-resolved false vetoes, while preserving 589/589 right-of-way respect, zero priority-agent false positives, and 400/400 negative-stress vetoes. We prove certificate soundness, structural right-of-way respect, exact finite-lattice minimality, fallback contingency, and blame-consistency conditions. CARVE does not predict or require another driver's compliance; it certifies whether a proposed interaction is bounded, attributable, and normatively admissible under declared assumptions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CARVE, a prediction-free certificate layer for autonomous driving that identifies bounded multi-agent "repairs" to recover maneuvers vetoed by hard safety rules, assigning responsibility, fallback, and normative admissibility without requiring prediction of other drivers' compliance.
AI.motivation: Existing rule-aware autonomous-driving stacks (rulebooks, shields, reachability filters) are good at vetoing unsafe actions, and prediction-based planners model likely responses, but neither provides a runtime proof object specifying which bounded multi-agent edit can repair an infeasible maneuver, who owns the repair, whether the request respects right-of-way, and what ego fallback remains. This gap causes legitimate interactive maneuvers to be unnecessarily rejected.
AI.method: The authors formulate "interactive repair certification" and propose CARVE, a prediction-free certificate layer built over a finite lattice of ego-owned and agent-owned tactical operators. Agent-owned requests are constrained within a cooperation envelope B_j(s) = β(π_j)·α_j^max(s), separating kinematic reachability from normative priority. The resulting certificate records the binding rule, repair category, repair set, responsibility-weighted cost split, and fallback. The authors prove properties including certificate soundness, structural right-of-way respect, finite-lattice minimality, fallback contingency, and blame-consistency.
AI.result: Evaluated on 589 Lanelet2-geometry-grounded INTERACTION replay episodes, CARVE-Greedy accepts 98.64% of initially vetoed maneuvers and recovers 370/378 human-resolved false vetoes, while preserving 589/589 right-of-way respect, zero priority-agent false positives, and 400/400 negative-stress vetoes.
AI.conclusion: CARVE provides a principled, prediction-free certification framework that determines whether a proposed interactive maneuver is bounded, attributable, and normatively admissible. It bridges the gap between hard safety vetoes and interactive feasibility without requiring compliance predictions from other agents, offering provably sound certificates with practical near-complete recovery of false vetoes on real-world data.

title: A Novel Procedural Generation for Level Design of Mansions and Dungeons
summary: Procedural Content Generation (PCG) has become an essential technique in game development due to its ability to reduce production time and cost while increasing replayability and variety. However, when not aligned with level design principles, PCG can lead to incoherent spatial structures and poor gameplay experiences. Objective: This work proposes a PCG method guided by level design principles to generate structured indoor environments - such as houses, mansions, and dungeons - aiming to ensure both architectural coherence and navigability. Methodology: The method is divided into three main stages: segmentation of the space using Binary Space Partitioning (BSP); logical connection of rooms based on graph traversal to prevent redundant links; and a post-processing stage responsible for cleaning structural artifacts and improving visual cohesion. The methodology allows parameterization of room area and shape, with randomness controlled via seeds for reproducibility. Results: Two experiments were conducted. The first demonstrated the flexibility of the methodology under different seeds and parameter configurations. The second evaluated the navigability of generated maps by verifying connectivity using Breadth-First Search (BFS). In this test, 100,000 maps were generated, and with suitable parameters, over 91% of them achieved complete connectivity.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a PCG method guided by level design principles to generate coherent and navigable indoor environments (houses, mansions, dungeons) using Binary Space Partitioning (BSP), graph-based logical connections, and post-processing. Experimental results show the method's flexibility and achieves over 91% complete connectivity in 100,000 generated maps.
AI.motivation: Procedural Content Generation (PCG) reduces production time and cost while increasing replayability, but without proper alignment with level design principles, it can create incoherent spatial structures and poor gameplay experiences. This work aims to address this by integrating level design principles into PCG to ensure architectural coherence and navigability.
AI.method: The method consists of three stages: (1) space segmentation using Binary Space Partitioning (BSP); (2) logical connection of rooms via graph traversal to prevent redundant links; and (3) post-processing to clean structural artifacts and improve visual cohesion. The methodology allows parameterization of room area and shape with randomness controlled via seeds for reproducibility.
AI.result: Two experiments were conducted. The first demonstrated flexibility under different seeds and parameter configurations. The second evaluated navigability using Breadth-First Search (BFS) on 100,000 generated maps, finding that with suitable parameters, over 91% achieved complete connectivity.
AI.conclusion: The proposed PCG method successfully integrates level design principles to generate structured, coherent, and navigable indoor environments, demonstrating high connectivity rates (over 91%) and flexibility across different parameter configurations. This validates the effectiveness of combining BSP, graph-based connections, and post-processing for producing high-quality procedural level designs.

title: D2MDT: Department-aware Multidisciplinary Team Consultation with Deliberation for Efficient Clinical Prediction
summary: Electronic health records (EHRs) are central to clinical prediction, but existing methods either rely on correlation-driven deep models or use single large language models (LLMs), making it difficult to support multidisciplinary clinical reasoning. Recent multi-agent systems (MAS) provide a promising alternative, yet current EHR-grounded MAS methods still suffer from weak evidence differentiation across agents and redundant multi-round interaction. We propose D2MDT, a Department-aware MultiDisciplinary Team Consultation with Deliberation for Efficient clinical prediction. D2MDT first constructs structured EHR evidence and consultation-ready semantic evidence for multi-agent consultation. It then assigns patient-specific department perspectives to doctor agents and retrieves complementary evidence for collaborative consultation. To improve efficiency, D2MDT further introduces residual deliberation, which updates only unresolved consensus rather than replaying the full discussion history. Finally, D2MDT fuses the refined consensus report with structured EHR representations for prediction. Experiments on mortality prediction show that D2MDT improves both predictive performance and consultation efficiency. We release the code online to ease the reproducibility of this paper.

AI.tldr: D2MDT is a department-aware multi-disciplinary team consultation framework with deliberation that leverages multi-agent LLM systems on structured EHR data for efficient and accurate clinical (mortality) prediction.
AI.motivation: Existing EHR-based clinical prediction methods either rely on correlation-driven deep models or single LLMs, failing to support multidisciplinary clinical reasoning. Current EHR-grounded multi-agent systems (MAS) suffer from weak evidence differentiation across agents and redundant multi-round interactions, limiting their practicality.
AI.method: D2MDT (1) constructs structured EHR evidence and consultation-ready semantic evidence for multi-agent consultation; (2) assigns patient-specific department perspectives to doctor agents and retrieves complementary evidence for collaborative consultation; (3) introduces residual deliberation, updating only unresolved consensus instead of replaying full discussion history to improve efficiency; and (4) fuses the refined consensus report with structured EHR representations for final prediction.
AI.result: Experiments on mortality prediction demonstrate that D2MDT improves both predictive performance and consultation efficiency compared to existing approaches. Code is released for reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: D2MDT effectively bridges multidisciplinary clinical reasoning and EHR-based prediction by combining structured evidence, department-aware multi-agent consultation, and efficient residual deliberation, achieving superior and more efficient clinical predictions.

title: Fixed-Time Dynamic Landing of Quadrotors using Adaptive Unscented Kalman Filtering and Nonlinear Model Predictive Control
comment: Accepted to the Conference on Robots and Vision (CRV 2026), Vancouver, Canada
summary: This paper introduces an estimation and control framework for dynamic landing of multi-rotor uncrewed aerial vehicles on moving platforms. The proposed method integrates nonlinear model predictive control with a real-time minimum-jerk trajectory planner that enforces a prescribed touchdown time, enabling consistent timing during the terminal descent. To enhance robustness in the presence of time-varying sensing quality, we utilize an adaptive unscented kalman filter that updates the process and measurement noise statistics online. In addition, we provide a reference feasibility analysis showing that minimum-jerk references induce bounded thrust and torque commands under standard tracking hypotheses. The proposed framework is evaluated in simulation and hardware experiments, and it is shown to achieve repeatable landings and improved platform velocity prediction accuracy relative to EKF/UKF-based methods.

title: ModuLoop : Low-Level Code Generation using Modular Synthesizer and Closed-Loop Debugger for Robotic Control
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance across various domains, including code generation and problem solving. However, their application in robotic control, particularly in low-level tasks that require precise manipulation, real-time feedback, and environment-dependent execution, remains limited. To address this challenge, we propose the Closed-Loop Modular Code Synthesizer framework. This framework leverages a pre-trained LLM without any task-specific fine-tuning to perform modular code planning and generation, and iteratively executes the generated code while inserting debugging probes to observe its behavior. This closed-loop structure facilitates systematic debugging and refinement, ultimately producing executable control programs. We apply the proposed framework to the calibration of an RGB-D camera and a robotic arm, validating its effectiveness in real-world settings. Furthermore, through a subsequent pick-and-place task, we demonstrate not only the accuracy of the calibration but also the potential extensibility of the framework. Across both tasks, the framework achieved high execution accuracy and autonomy, illustrating the practicality and scalability of LLM-based robotic control using our framework.

AI.tldr: A closed-loop framework using pre-trained LLMs for modular code planning and generation in robotic control, enabling iterative debugging and refinement without task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: LLMs have shown impressive performance across domains but remain limited in robotic control applications, particularly for low-level tasks requiring precise manipulation, real-time feedback, and environment-dependent execution.
AI.method: The Closed-Loop Modular Code Synthesizer framework leverages pre-trained LLMs (without task-specific fine-tuning) to perform modular code planning and generation, iteratively executes the generated code while inserting debugging probes to observe behavior, and uses a closed-loop structure for systematic debugging and refinement to produce executable control programs.
AI.result: Applied to RGB-D camera calibration and robotic arm calibration, the framework achieved high execution accuracy and autonomy in real-world settings, with demonstrated extensibility through a pick-and-place task showing its potential for broader robotic control applications.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates the practicality and scalability of LLM-based robotic control, achieving both accuracy and autonomy while maintaining a modular approach that can be extended to various control tasks.

title: Motion Planning in Dynamic Environments: A Survey from Classical to Modern Methods
summary: Motion planning in dynamic environments requires robots to continuously adapt their paths in response to environmental changes for safe and uninterrupted navigation. While many surveys have reviewed planning in static settings, systematic reviews focused on dynamic environments remain limited. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of 138 works, primarily published between 2015 and 2025, spanning both classical and learning-based approaches. The motion planning methods are grouped into five categories based on the concepts of sampling, graph search, model predictive control, learning, and additional classical local planning approaches, including velocity obstacles, potential fields and dynamic windows. The learning techniques include supervised learning and reinforcement learning. We also discuss the role of dynamic perception in motion planning, covering techniques for detecting and modeling moving obstacles using cameras, LiDAR, and event-based sensors. The survey analyzes the principles, strengths, and limitations of each method, with particular attention to challenges unique to dynamic environments, such as prediction uncertainty, human-robot interaction, and the freezing robot problem. The survey provides researchers with a structured understanding of motion planning methods in dynamic environments.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey of 138 works (2015–2025) reviewing motion planning methods for robots in dynamic environments, covering classical approaches (sampling, graph search, MPC, velocity obstacles, potential fields, dynamic windows) and learning-based approaches (supervised learning, reinforcement learning), along with dynamic perception techniques and challenges unique to dynamic settings.
AI.motivation: Motion planning in dynamic environments requires continuous path adaptation for safe navigation. While many surveys cover static environment planning, systematic reviews focused specifically on dynamic environments remain limited, motivating this comprehensive survey.
AI.method: The survey reviews 138 works (primarily 2015–2025) and categorizes motion planning methods into five groups: sampling-based, graph search-based, model predictive control (MPC), learning-based (supervised and reinforcement learning), and additional classical local planning approaches (velocity obstacles, potential fields, dynamic windows). It also discusses dynamic perception techniques using cameras, LiDAR, and event-based sensors for detecting and modeling moving obstacles.
AI.result: The survey provides a structured analysis of the principles, strengths, and limitations of each method category, with particular focus on challenges unique to dynamic environments such as prediction uncertainty, human-robot interaction, and the freezing robot problem.
AI.conclusion: The survey equips researchers with a structured and comprehensive understanding of motion planning methods in dynamic environments, bridging the gap left by prior surveys focused on static settings, and highlights open challenges and future research directions.

title: See Less, Specify More: Visual Evidence Budgets for Generalizable VLAs
summary:
Generalization remains a central bottleneck for vision-language-action (VLA) models: under distractors, appearance shifts, and semantically similar tasks, the policy must often infer local execution details from coarse instructions while also deciding which parts of the image matter for control. We present S2 (See Less, Specify More), a framework for improving VLA generalization by training the executor under a cleaner interface.
  Specify More preserves the original instruction as a stable high-level goal while relabeling each trajectory into refined trajectory- and subtask-level language that disambiguates the current execution mode. Unlike native attention, See Less imposes an explicit visual evidence budget, training the executor to act from task-sufficient evidence rather than unconstrained visual context, without any region or mask annotation.
  This interface lets the executor follow detailed guidance without relying on distracting visual patches or resolving avoidable ambiguity on its own, and it remains compatible with off-the-shelf VLM planners through in-context learning. Across our main evaluation settings, S2 improves overall generalization metrics by changing the executor's learning problem: coarse instructions induce avoidable supervision aliasing, goal-preserving local guidance outperforms instruction replacement in our main ablations, and explicit evidence budgeting reduces dependence on broad visual context beyond efficiency considerations.
  Across eight real-robot tasks on TX-G2 (an AgiBot G2-compatible variant) and HSR, S2 raises mean subtask success from 54.2% to 79.0% over pi0.5. Together, these results suggest that VLA generalization improves when the executor is trained to act from informative local guidance and task-sufficient visual evidence, rather than recovering both from weak supervision.

AI.tldr: S2 (See Less, Specify More) improves VLA generalization by training the executor under a cleaner interface with explicit visual evidence budget and refined trajectory- and subtask-level language guidance.
AI.motivation: Generalization remains a bottleneck for VLA models, which must infer local execution details from coarse instructions while deciding what parts of the image matter for control under distractors, appearance shifts, and semantically similar tasks.
AI.method: S2 combines two key components: (1) Specify More - preserves original instruction as stable high-level goal while relabeling trajectories into refined trajectory- and subtask-level language; (2) See Less - imposes explicit visual evidence budget, training executor to act from task-sufficient evidence rather than unconstrained visual context. Compatible with off-the-shelf VLM planners through in-context learning.
AI.result: Across eight real-robot tasks on TX-G2 and HSR, S2 raises mean subtask success from 54.2% (pi0.5) to 79.0%, demonstrating significant improvement in overall generalization metrics.
AI.conclusion: VLA generalization improves when the executor is trained to act from informative local guidance and task-sufficient visual evidence, rather than recovering both from weak supervision.

title: SeeTraceAct: Visibility-Aware Latent Planning from Cross-Embodiment Demonstration Videos
summary: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) are promising general-purpose robot policies, but adapting them to new tasks typically requires costly task-specific teleoperation data. As an alternative, we study one-shot demo-conditioned VLAs, where a robot policy is conditioned on a single demonstration video of an unseen task. We find that existing end-to-end approaches often struggle when successful execution requires precisely localizing small target regions. To address this limitation, we propose SeeTraceAct, a demo-conditioned VLA framework that encourages precise spatial grounding through visibility-aware prediction of future end-effector traces. To enable reproducible evaluation with cross-embodiment demonstrations, we introduce and release RoboCasa-DC, a demo-conditioned extension of RoboCasa with episode-paired humanoid videos. Experiments on RoboCasa-DC and a real-world benchmark, where a Franka Panda arm is conditioned on human demonstrations, show that SeeTraceAct outperforms baselines, achieving the best success rate across all four RoboCasa-DC settings and improving real-world average success by 12.5 percentage points.

AI.tldr: SeeTraceAct is a demo-conditioned vision-language-action model that enables one-shot task adaptation by predicting visibility-aware future end-effector traces, achieving superior performance over existing methods in both simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) are promising general-purpose robot policies but require costly task-specific teleoperation data for adaptation. Existing end-to-end VLA approaches struggle when successful execution requires precisely localizing small target regions.
AI.method: SeeTraceAct introduces a demo-conditioned VLA framework that encourages precise spatial grounding through visibility-aware prediction of future end-effector traces. The authors also introduce RoboCasa-DC, a demo-conditioned extension of RoboCasa with episode-paired humanoid videos for reproducible cross-embodiment evaluation.
AI.result: SeeTraceAct outperforms baselines across all four RoboCasa-DC settings and improves real-world average success by 12.5 percentage points when conditioning on human demonstrations for a Franka Panda arm.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method effectively addresses the limitation of precise spatial grounding in one-shot demo-conditioned VLAs, demonstrating superior performance in both simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks.

title: Hybrid Adaptive Kalman Filtering for Data-Efficient Joint Tracking and Classification
summary: Kalman filtering performance is highly sensitive to model mismatch and noise covariance tuning. Learning-based approaches address these limitations but typically rely on supervised training with large datasets and do not produce consistent uncertainty estimates. In this paper, we propose a self-supervised Hybrid Adaptive Kalman Filter that learns structured corrections to system dynamics and process noise covariance from measurements alone while preserving the probabilistic structure of the filter. This allows the innovation likelihood to be computed and subsequently used for model classification via generalized Bayesian inference. Experimental results on real-world and simulated datasets demonstrate improved estimation accuracy and statistical consistency as well as robust classification performance across both low-data and large-data scenarios.

AI.tldr: A self-supervised Hybrid Adaptive Kalman Filter is proposed that learns structured corrections to system dynamics and process noise covariance from measurements alone, preserving probabilistic consistency and enabling model classification via generalized Bayesian inference.
AI.motivation: Classical Kalman filtering is highly sensitive to model mismatch and noise covariance tuning. Existing learning-based alternatives typically require large supervised datasets and fail to produce consistent uncertainty estimates.
AI.method: The proposed Hybrid Adaptive Kalman Filter learns structured corrections to system dynamics and process noise covariance in a self-supervised manner using only measurements, while preserving the filter's probabilistic structure. The innovation likelihood is computed and leveraged for model classification through generalized Bayesian inference.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world and simulated datasets show improved estimation accuracy, statistical consistency, and robust classification performance in both low-data and large-data scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The approach effectively bridges classical Kalman filtering and learning-based methods by achieving adaptive, self-supervised corrections with consistent uncertainty estimates and strong classification capabilities, without reliance on large labeled datasets.

title: A Measurement-Driven Digital Twin Architecture for Plant-Level Biomass Estimation and Growth Forecasting in Hydroponic Systems
summary: Alternatives to soil-based horticulture, such as hydroponics, have been developed to respond to food distribution concerns for dense urban centers. A new system was developed to track an individual lettuce plant's growth in a hydroponic environment, utilizing streams of measured information and available models to continuously update the growth trajectory estimates for a plant. These "digital twin" models were integrated into an operating hydroponic greenhouse, with custom horticultural and sensor hardware to grow and measure relevant information. To aid in updating model parameters, plant yield was continuously measured with a custom neural network, using RGB-D images of the plants as an input. The network, trained on a collected dataset of 1300 images, was able to estimate mass within 1.5 g of the ground-truth value. After integration into the custom system, digital twin growth projections could approximate future yield between one and four days in the future, maintaining around a 2 g forecasting error.

AI.tldr: A digital twin system was developed for hydroponic lettuce, combining sensor data, growth models, and a custom neural network for non-destructive yield estimation, achieving ~2 g forecasting error for 1–4 day yield projections.
AI.motivation: Urban food distribution challenges have driven interest in soil-free horticulture alternatives like hydroponics. There is a need for real-time monitoring and predictive modeling of individual plant growth in hydroponic environments to improve yield management and operational decision-making.
AI.method: The authors built a custom hydroponic greenhouse system with integrated horticultural and sensor hardware. A "digital twin" model was developed to continuously update individual plant growth trajectory estimates using measured data streams and available growth models. To non-destructively estimate plant mass, a custom neural network was trained on a dataset of 1,300 RGB-D images. The system was deployed and tested in an operational hydroponic greenhouse setting.
AI.result: The neural network estimated plant mass within 1.5 g of ground-truth values. After full system integration, the digital twin growth projections approximated future yield 1–4 days ahead with approximately 2 g forecasting error.
AI.conclusion: The integration of digital twin models with RGB-D image-based neural network yield estimation provides an effective framework for real-time, individual-plant-level growth tracking and short-term yield forecasting in hydroponic systems, demonstrating practical viability for smart urban agriculture.

title: Direct Informed Sampling on Riemannian Manifolds via Loewner Order Lower Bounds
comment: Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary: Informed sampling techniques accelerate sampling-based motion planners by focusing the search on promising regions of the state space, yet most existing methods rely on Euclidean heuristics that become inadmissible under configuration-dependent Riemannian metrics. While scalar eigenvalue bounds restore admissibility by uniformly scaling the Euclidean distance, they discard the directional structure of the metric, producing overly conservative informed sets. We propose a matrix-valued admissible heuristic that exploits the Loewner order on symmetric positive definite matrices to compute the tightest constant lower bound on the metric tensor while preserving its full directional structure. The Cholesky factorization of this bound defines a linear map to an isotropic Euclidean space in which the Riemannian informed set reduces to a standard prolate hyperspheroid, enabling direct, rejection-free sampling using existing algorithms. Experiments on manipulation tasks with a 6-DoF UR5, 7-DoF Franka, and 14-DoF PR2 under three distinct Riemannian metrics show that our heuristic produces consistently tighter informed sets than both the Euclidean and scalar eigenvalue bounds, accelerating convergence across multiple state-of-the-art asymptotically optimal planners.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a matrix-valued admissible heuristic for sampling-based motion planning that uses Loewner order to compute tight bounds on Riemannian metrics, enabling more efficient sampling than existing Euclidean or scalar eigenvalue bounds.
AI.motivation: Existing informed sampling techniques rely on Euclidean heuristics that become inadmissible under configuration-dependent Riemannian metrics. While scalar eigenvalue bounds restore admissibility, they discard directional structure of the metric, producing overly conservative informed sets.
AI.method: The authors propose a matrix-valued admissible heuristic exploiting the Loewner order on symmetric positive definite matrices to compute the tightest constant lower bound on the metric tensor while preserving its full directional structure. The Cholesky factorization of this bound defines a linear map to an isotropic Euclidean space where the Riemannian informed set becomes a standard prolate hyperspheroid, enabling direct rejection-free sampling.
AI.result: Experiments on UR5 (6-DoF), Franka (7-DoF), and PR2 (14-DoF) robots under three distinct Riemannian metrics demonstrate that the proposed heuristic produces consistently tighter informed sets than both Euclidean and scalar eigenvalue bounds, accelerating convergence across multiple state-of-the-art asymptotically optimal planners.
AI.conclusion: The matrix-valued heuristic provides a more efficient approach to informed sampling under Riemannian metrics for motion planning, balancing admissibility with computational efficiency through tighter informed sets that preserve directional information.

title: Impact of a Soft Wearable Back-Support Device on Postural Stability during Trip-Like Perturbations
comment: 6 pages, 6 figures, to be published in the proceedings of the 2026 11th IEEE RAS/EMBS International Conference for Biomedical Robotics and Biomechatronics (BioRob)
summary: The effectiveness of a soft wearable back-support device in enhancing postural stability was investigated under trip-like perturbations using two experimental paradigms: perturbed standing and perturbed walking. Healthy subjects completed trials under three different back-support conditions: no device, device worn with low stiffness, and device activated with high stiffness. Whole-body stability was quantified using the minimum Margin of Stability (MOS) at the point of maximal instability. Results demonstrated increased MOS during device use, indicating enhanced postural stability. In standing, MOS increased significantly with device stiffness, whereas in walking, both device conditions improved MOS relative to no device but did not differ significantly from each other. These findings highlight the potential of soft wearable back-support devices with adjustable stiffness to improve reactive balance control against external perturbations, with important implications for fall prevention. Future research should explore personalized stiffness optimization and evaluate efficacy in populations at elevated risk of falls.

AI.tldr: Soft wearable back-support devices with adjustable stiffness improve postural stability under trip-like perturbations in both standing and walking, as measured by the Margin of Stability (MOS), suggesting potential for fall prevention.
AI.motivation: Falls due to external perturbations (e.g., trips) are a significant safety concern. There is a need to investigate whether soft wearable back-support devices with adjustable stiffness can enhance reactive balance control and reduce fall risk.
AI.method: Two experimental paradigms—perturbed standing and perturbed walking—were used with healthy subjects under three back-support conditions: no device, low stiffness, and high stiffness. Whole-body postural stability was quantified using the minimum Margin of Stability (MOS) at the point of maximal instability.
AI.result: Device use increased MOS, indicating enhanced postural stability. In standing, MOS increased significantly with device stiffness. In walking, both low and high stiffness conditions improved MOS compared to no device, but no significant difference was found between the two stiffness levels.
AI.conclusion: Soft wearable back-support devices with adjustable stiffness show promise for improving reactive balance control against trip-like perturbations, with implications for fall prevention. Future work should focus on personalized stiffness optimization and testing in populations at elevated fall risk.

title: Improved Postural Stability Using a Lightweight Semi-Active Soft Back Support Device Under Standing Perturbations
comment: 6 pages, 8 figures, submitted to IROS 2026, the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems
summary: Older adults are particularly susceptible to falls following perturbations during standing, such as forward loss of balance. Back support devices that assist trunk extension may help mitigate fall risk by preventing excessive trunk flexion. Previous studies have investigated heavy back support devices; however, these systems often introduced adverse effects on stability due to their added mass, which shifted the body's natural center of mass unfavorably. In contrast, lightweight passive devices have shown limited benefits, as they can generate only modest assistive forces during the relatively small trunk flexion associated with forward balance loss. In this study, we evaluated the effects of a lightweight semi-active soft back support device on postural stability following standing perturbations. Our device combines an active element (a pneumatic artificial muscle) in parallel with a passive elastic band. The active element rapidly provides assistive force following a perturbation, overcoming the limitations of passive devices. Experiments conducted with five healthy individuals demonstrated that the semi-active device significantly reduced whole-body angular momentum and increased the margin of stability, indicating improved balance recovery performance. These results highlight the promise of semi-active soft wearable robots as an effective and lightweight strategy for fall prevention during standing perturbations.

AI.tldr: A lightweight semi-active soft back support device combining a pneumatic artificial muscle with a passive elastic band significantly improved postural stability and balance recovery in healthy individuals following standing perturbations, offering a promising fall prevention strategy for older adults.
AI.motivation: Older adults are vulnerable to falls from forward loss of balance during standing. Existing heavy back support devices shift the body's center of mass and impair stability, while lightweight passive devices generate insufficient assistive force during the small trunk flexion typical of forward balance loss. A solution that is both lightweight and capable of rapid force assistance is needed.
AI.method: The authors developed a lightweight semi-active soft back support device that pairs an active pneumatic artificial muscle in parallel with a passive elastic band. The active element rapidly delivers assistive force upon perturbation, compensating for the force limitations of purely passive systems. The device was experimentally evaluated on five healthy individuals subjected to standing perturbations, assessing whole-body angular momentum and margin of stability.
AI.result: The semi-active device significantly reduced whole-body angular momentum and increased the margin of stability compared to unsupported conditions, demonstrating improved balance recovery performance following perturbations.
AI.conclusion: Semi-active soft wearable robots represent an effective and lightweight strategy for fall prevention during standing perturbations, overcoming the trade-offs between device mass and assistive force seen in both heavy active and lightweight passive back support systems.

title: SCOPE: Real-Time Natural Language Camera Agent at the Edge
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Accepted at HRI '26 (21st ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction), Edinburgh, Scotland, March 16--19, 2026. Code: https://github.com/HindsboNikolaj/SCOPE
summary:
Deploying language-driven agents in robotics requires evaluations that reflect real-world task demands: natural-language instructions with reproducible outcomes. Such agents must connect language models to callable perception and control tools, and be assessed using deployment-critical metrics including latency, accuracy, and error modes. We present SCOPE (Simulation and Camera Operations for Perception and Evaluation), a modular agent for natural-language, open-vocabulary pan-tilt-zoom (PTZ) camera control and visual scene understanding, designed explicitly for edge deployment. SCOPE operates both in a Blender-based simulation environment and on a physical PTZ camera, executing all perception, planning, and control locally at the deployment site using edge-accessible compute.
  We release a 536-task benchmark spanning QA, single- and multi-step commands, counting, spatial reasoning, descriptions, and optical character recognition in a Blender-based simulation environment that exposes realistic PTZ control affordances. Execution traces are combined with an LM-as-Judge to evaluate latency, accuracy, and error modes.
  We evaluate 19 planner-perception model combinations pairing Qwen3 small language models (SLMs) with Moondream and Qwen vision-language models (VLMs). Stronger SLMs substantially reduce hallucinations and improve tool routing, leading to more reliable closed-loop behavior. Once a sufficiently capable SLM is used, perception becomes the dominant performance bottleneck. Mixture-of-Experts models on both the planning and perception side consistently match or exceed dense alternatives at latencies and memory footprints comparable to much smaller networks. Quantization provides additional efficiency gains with minimal accuracy degradation, identifying a practical, sim-to-real validated design point for real-time, edge-feasible language-driven PTZ control.

AI.tldr: SCOPE is a modular, edge-deployable agent for natural-language PTZ camera control and visual scene understanding, featuring a 536-task Blender benchmark and demonstrating that stronger small language models reduce hallucinations while perception becomes the bottleneck, with MoE and quantization providing efficiency gains.
AI.motivation: Deploying language-driven agents in robotics requires evaluations that reflect real-world task demands: natural-language instructions with reproducible outcomes. Agents must connect language models to callable perception and control tools and be assessed using deployment-critical metrics including latency, accuracy, and error modes.
AI.method: SCOPE (Simulation and Camera Operations for Perception and Evaluation) is a modular agent for natural-language, open-vocabulary pan-tilt-zoom (PTZ) camera control and visual scene understanding designed explicitly for edge deployment. It operates in both Blender-based simulation and on physical PTZ cameras, executing all perception, planning, and control locally at the deployment site. The authors release a 536-task benchmark spanning QA, multi-step commands, counting, spatial reasoning, descriptions, and OCR. Execution traces are combined with an LM-as-Judge to evaluate latency, accuracy, and error modes.
AI.result: 19 planner-perception model combinations were evaluated pairing Qwen3 small language models (SLMs) with Moondream and Qwen vision-language models (VLMs). Stronger SLMs substantially reduce hallucinations and improve tool routing. Once a sufficiently capable SLM is used, perception becomes the dominant performance bottleneck. Mixture-of-Experts models on both planning and perception consistently match or exceed dense alternatives at comparable latencies and memory footprints. Quantization provides additional efficiency gains with minimal accuracy degradation.
AI.conclusion: The study identifies a practical, sim-to-real validated design point for real-time, edge-feasible language-driven PTZ control, demonstrating that with appropriate model selection (strong SLM + MoE architecture + quantization), effective language-driven camera control is achievable on edge devices.

title: Hybrid Dynamics Modeling for a Flexible 2-DoF Robotic Arm
summary: This paper examines three approaches for modeling the dynamics of a flexible-link 2-DoF robotic arm to address unmodeled dynamics not captured by rigid-body models. Two physics informed models combine rigid-body dynamics (RBD) formulations with a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) to capture residual model errors and linkage flexibility. A kinematics-based regression model serves as a purely data-driven baseline. Using an open-source dataset, torque predictions are first estimated using Ridge regression on kinematic features, while the physicsbased baseline is constructed from published specifications, and ordinary least-squares regression is subsequently used to estimate the same parameter set directly from data. Results show that the physics-based parameters yield the poorest accuracy, while regularized and least-squares estimators align more closely with measured torques. Residual analysis and error metrics highlight the limitations of purely parametric models for flexible-link systems and underscore the value of regularization and data-driven identification, supporting developments of semi-parametric residual learning methods.

AI.tldr: This paper compares three modeling approaches for flexible-link robotic arm dynamics: two physics-informed models combining rigid-body dynamics with Gaussian Mixture Models and one data-driven kinematics-based regression model. Using an open-source dataset, the study finds that physics-based parameters perform poorest in accuracy, while regularized and least-squares estimators align more closely with measured torques, highlighting limitations of purely parametric models.
AI.motivation: To address unmodeled dynamics not captured by rigid-body models in flexible-link 2-DoF robotic arms by comparing physics-informed and data-driven approaches.
AI.method: Three modeling approaches: (1) Physics-informed model 1: rigid-body dynamics + Gaussian Mixture Model; (2) Physics-informed model 2: rigid-body dynamics + Gaussian Mixture Model; (3) Kinematics-based regression (data-driven). Methodology: using open-source dataset, torque predictions estimated via Ridge regression on kinematic features and ordinary least-squares regression on physics-based parameters.
AI.result: Physics-based parameters yielded poorest accuracy. Regularized and least-squares estimators aligned more closely with measured torques. Residual analysis and error metrics highlighted limitations of purely parametric models for flexible-link systems.
AI.conclusion: Regularization and data-driven identification provide better results than purely physics-based parameter estimation. Supports development of semi-parametric residual learning methods that combine physics-based modeling with data-driven approaches.

title: MARIO: Motion-Augmented Real-Time Multi-Sensor Inertial Odometry
summary: Inertial odometry (IO) using only Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) provides a lightweight solution for human motion tracking in augmented reality (AR) and wearable devices. Recent learning-based IO methods have improved the generalizability of inertial localization through large-scale pretraining on human motion datasets. However, these approaches remain prone to drift and noise because they do not explicitly capture human motion dynamics, especially on daily activity datasets such as Nymeria. In this work, we propose to ground inertial odometry in human kinematics through a learned IMU-inferred pose prior, which promotes physically consistent motion constraints. We integrate this pose prior into existing IO architectures and reduce positional drift by up to 36% on the challenging Nymeria dataset, which is 5x larger than datasets used in prior work. We further improve long-term performance with a sensor-fusion framework that incorporates auxiliary signals from lightweight sensors already available on commercial AR glasses, including magnetometers, barometers, and secondary IMUs. With this fusion strategy, positional drift is reduced by up to 42%, improving robustness and generalization across diverse motion conditions. Together, our results introduce a new paradigm for inertial and lightweight odometry by unifying human motion kinematics with multimodal sensing, setting a new benchmark for accurate and robust camera-less human tracking. Our website is available at https://spice-lab.org/projects/MARIO/.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes MARIO, a method that grounds inertial odometry (IO) in human kinematics via a learned IMU-inferred pose prior and integrates lightweight auxiliary sensors (magnetometers, barometers, secondary IMUs) on AR glasses, reducing positional drift by up to 42% on the large-scale Nymeria dataset.
AI.motivation: Existing learning-based inertial odometry methods suffer from drift and noise because they do not explicitly model human motion dynamics. This problem is especially pronounced on large-scale daily activity datasets such as Nymeria, limiting the reliability of camera-less human motion tracking in AR and wearable applications.
AI.method: The authors introduce a learned IMU-inferred pose prior that enforces physically consistent human kinematic constraints, and integrate it into existing IO architectures. They further propose a sensor-fusion framework that leverages auxiliary lightweight sensors commonly available on commercial AR glasses—magnetometers, barometers, and secondary IMUs—to enhance long-term odometry performance.
AI.result: On the Nymeria dataset (5× larger than prior datasets), the pose prior alone reduces positional drift by up to 36%. Combining the pose prior with the multimodal sensor-fusion strategy further reduces positional drift by up to 42%, demonstrating improved robustness and generalization across diverse motion conditions.
AI.conclusion: Unifying human motion kinematics with multimodal lightweight sensing establishes a new paradigm for camera-less inertial odometry, setting a new benchmark for accurate and robust human tracking in AR and wearable device scenarios.

title: TTT-VLA: Test-Time Latent Prompt Optimization for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models trained on large-scale data have made remarkable progress, but they remain vulnerable to distribution shifts at deployment time. Recent VLA models suggest that prompts can serve as an efficient interface for steering policy behavior, but existing prompt-based steering typically relies on external guidance. This raises a natural question: can test-time training (TTT) for VLA be achieved by optimizing a prompt, so that the steering interface itself can be learned and adapted from interaction? We address this question with TTT-VLA, a test-time training framework based on Latent Prompt Optimization (LPO). During training, the latent prompt is learned with an additional proxy task, providing an extra learned conditioning signal for policy learning. At test time, TTT is performed by collecting interaction data from the current environment and optimizing only the latent prompt on those data using the proxy task's self-supervised signal, without modifying the policy itself. Experiments on SimplerEnv demonstrate that the proposed method consistently improves task success rates in both single- and multi-embodiment settings. Further analysis shows that the gains arise primarily from correcting a small number of critical decisions rather than globally altering policy behavior. These results suggest that LPO provides an effective and practical pathway for deployment-time improvement of foundation manipulation policies.

AI.tldr: TTT-VLA is a test-time training framework for Vision-Language-Action models that adapts to deployment-time distribution shifts by optimizing a latent prompt via a proxy self-supervised task, improving task success rates without modifying the underlying policy.
AI.motivation: VLA models trained at scale are vulnerable to distribution shifts at deployment. Existing prompt-based steering methods rely on external guidance, raising the question of whether test-time adaptation can be achieved by learning the steering prompt itself from interaction data.
AI.method: The paper proposes TTT-VLA, built on Latent Prompt Optimization (LPO). During training, a latent prompt is jointly learned with an additional proxy task that provides an extra conditioning signal. At test time, interaction data is collected from the current environment and used to optimize only the latent prompt via the proxy task's self-supervised signal, leaving the policy network itself unchanged.
AI.result: Experiments on SimplerEnv show consistent improvements in task success rates across both single- and multi-embodiment settings. Analysis reveals that performance gains stem primarily from correcting a small number of critical decisions rather than globally reshaping policy behavior.
AI.conclusion: Latent Prompt Optimization offers an effective and practical pathway for deployment-time improvement of foundation manipulation policies, enabling test-time adaptation through prompt-level optimization without requiring policy retraining.

title: How Visible Are Silent Manipulation Failures? An Observability Study of False-Success Detection in Simulated Robot Episodes
summary: Imitation-learning policies for robot manipulation inherit the quality of the success labels attached to their training episodes, and those labels are usually produced by the robot's own success check. A particularly damaging error is the false success: an episode the robot logs as a success when the task outcome was actually wrong. We ask a narrow but practical question about these episodes. Once an episode has already been flagged as a success, how much of the information needed to overturn that label is present in proprioception, and how much requires vision? We build a simulated testbed on two bimanual ALOHA tasks, induce failures through environment perturbations rather than label edits, label every episode by privileged simulator state that the detector never sees, and keep only episodes the robot flagged as successful. We then compare detectors restricted to proprioception against a vision-based detector. We find that recoverability spans a wide range: in cube transfer the false successes are almost fully recoverable from joint data alone, while in peg insertion proprioception recovers only part of them and a vision detector closes most of the gap. We also show that the proprioceptive separability we measure rests on velocity differences far below any realistic sensor noise floor, so it is best read as an optimistic upper bound that a noiseless simulator inflates. We release the generation and evaluation pipeline.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how much information about false success labels in robot manipulation can be recovered from proprioception (joint data) versus vision, finding significant task-dependent differences in recoverability.
AI.motivation: False success labels in imitation learning are damaging because episodes flagged as successful but actually failing corrupt the robot's learning. The authors ask a practical question: once an episode is flagged as a success, how much information is needed to overturn that label - is it available through proprioception alone, or does vision require?
AI.method: Built a simulated testbed on two bimanual ALOHA tasks, induced failures via environment perturbations rather than label edits, labeled episodes using privileged simulator state, kept only episodes flagged as successful, and compared proprioception-only detectors against vision-based detectors.
AI.result: Recoverability spans a wide range: in cube transfer, false successes are almost fully recoverable from joint data alone; in peg insertion, proprioception recovers only part of them and vision closes most of the gap. Proprioceptive separability relies on velocity differences far below realistic sensor noise floor, indicating optimistic upper bound.
AI.conclusion: The recoverability of false success labels depends heavily on task type, with some being fully recoverable from proprioception alone and others requiring vision. This suggests that current simulation-based training may be overly optimistic about what can be learned from proprioceptive data alone.

title: ConTrack: Constrained Hand Motion Tracking with Adaptive Trade-off Control
summary: Human demonstrations provide strong priors for robot manipulation, yet it is non-trivial to transfer them to execute on real robots due to the kinematic gap. In dexterous manipulation, it remains challenging to track long-horizon, contact-rich sequences even in simulators: a reference-tracking policy must keep objects on their target trajectories while preserving demonstrated joint motion and contact timing. Existing approaches often rely on hand-crafted reward tuning that require per-sequence tuning and break under limited interaction budgets. We introduce ConTrack, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework that scales with tracking data. ConTrack treats object tracking as a constraint and allocates remaining control authority to motion fidelity, which allows it to adapt task--style trade-offs online using a dual-variable update. In addition, ConTrack also stabilizes long-horizon learning with an adaptive mid-trajectory reset library that reuses policy-reachable simulator states. Our qualitative and quantitative results in simulation tracking and real robot demonstrate that ConTrack improves success and object pose accuracy significantly over prior arts while preserving joint and contact fidelity. Website: https://www.lyt0112.com/projects/ConTrack.

AI.tldr: ConTrack is an RL framework for transferring human demonstrations to real robots in dexterous manipulation, treating object tracking as a constraint and optimizing motion fidelity with adaptive trade-offs and mid-trajectory resets.
AI.motivation: Transferring human demonstrations to real robots is difficult due to the kinematic gap. In dexterous manipulation, tracking long-horizon, contact-rich reference sequences is challenging—policies must maintain object trajectories while preserving joint motion and contact timing. Existing methods rely on hand-crafted, per-sequence reward tuning that fails under limited interaction budgets.
AI.method: ConTrack formulates object tracking as a constraint and allocates remaining control authority to motion fidelity. It adapts task-style trade-offs online via a dual-variable update. Additionally, it stabilizes long-horizon learning using an adaptive mid-trajectory reset library that reuses policy-reachable simulator states.
AI.result: Qualitative and quantitative evaluations in both simulation and real robot settings show that ConTrack significantly improves success rates and object pose accuracy over prior methods while preserving joint and contact fidelity.
AI.conclusion: ConTrack provides a scalable, data-driven RL framework for dexterous manipulation reference tracking that outperforms prior approaches by combining constrained optimization of object tracking with adaptive motion fidelity allocation and efficient trajectory reset strategies, enabling effective sim-to-real transfer of human demonstrations.

title: GeoSem-WAM: Geometry- and Semantic-Aware World Action Models
summary: Recent World Action Models (WAMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in embodied decision-making. However, whether their effectiveness stems from explicit future imagination during inference or representation learning induced by predictive training remains an open question. Emerging evidence suggests the primary advantage lies in learning robust latent representations rather than generating future observations at test time. Nevertheless, existing WAMs mainly rely on RGB-based future prediction, which provides limited structural and spatial understanding of complex environments. To address this, we propose a structured world modeling framework that enhances latent representations through geometric and semantic supervision. Alongside future RGB prediction, our model introduces two auxiliary prediction branches for future geometry and semantic representations, enabling it to jointly capture scene dynamics, spatial geometry, and semantic context within a unified latent space. Crucially, our approach preserves efficient inference by avoiding explicit future rollout or video generation at test time. Extensive experiments show that incorporating structured world supervision consistently improves action prediction accuracy, scene understanding, and robustness under challenging embodied scenarios, highlighting its potential for advancing scalable and efficient WAMs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a structured world modeling framework for World Action Models (WAMs) that enhances latent representations through geometric and semantic supervision, improving action prediction accuracy and scene understanding without requiring explicit future rollout during inference.
AI.motivation: World Action Models (WAMs) have shown impressive capabilities in embodied decision-making, but it's unclear whether their effectiveness stems from explicit future imagination or representation learning. Existing WAMs primarily rely on RGB-based future prediction, which provides limited structural and spatial understanding of complex environments, necessitating better scene representation for robust embodied AI.
AI.method: The authors propose a structured world modeling framework that introduces two auxiliary prediction branches alongside RGB prediction: future geometry and semantic representations. This enables joint capture of scene dynamics, spatial geometry, and semantic context within a unified latent space. Crucially, the approach preserves efficient inference by avoiding explicit future rollout or video generation at test time.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that incorporating structured world supervision consistently improves action prediction accuracy, scene understanding, and robustness under challenging embodied scenarios. The framework achieves these benefits while maintaining computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight the potential for advancing scalable and efficient World Action Models by emphasizing representation learning through structured supervision rather than explicit future generation, providing a foundation for more robust embodied AI systems.

title: Toward Gripper-Integrated Active Electrosense for Pre-Contact Sensing in Underwater Soft Grippers
comment: Extended abstract accepted to the IEEE ICRA 2026 Workshop on Manipulation Robustness
summary: Underwater manipulation often occurs under degraded visibility due to turbidity, glare, and gripper occlusion, limiting the reliability of vision-based perception during approach and grasping. In such settings, soft grippers are well suited for compliant interaction, but they typically lack an onboard pre-contact cue that can guide approach and closure when vision is unreliable. This extended abstract explores active electrosense as a lightweight sensing modality that can provide a proximity-like signal prior to contact by measuring perturbations of an applied electric field in conductive media. We instrument an octopus-inspired gripper with a discrete electrode layout and record multi-channel sensing voltages using off-the-shelf hardware. Simulation and tank experiments with a suspended conductive sphere show structured, object-dependent changes in the multi-electrode voltage readout relative to empty-water baselines, with detectability varying across excitation of 5 to 20 V and frequencies from 1 mHz to 1 kHz. These findings motivate systematic investigation of gripper-integrated electrosense as a complementary pre-contact cue for underwater soft manipulation.

AI.tldr: This paper explores using active electrosense (measuring electric field perturbations) as a lightweight sensing modality for underwater soft grippers to provide pre-contact proximity cues when vision is unreliable due to degraded visibility conditions.
AI.motivation: Underwater manipulation faces challenges from degraded visibility (turbidity, glare, gripper occlusion), which limits vision-based perception reliability. While soft grippers are well-suited for compliant underwater interaction, they typically lack onboard pre-contact cues that can guide approach and closure when vision is unreliable.
AI.method: The researchers instrument an octopus-inspired gripper with a discrete electrode layout and record multi-channel sensing voltages using off-the-shelf hardware. They perform both simulation and tank experiments using a suspended conductive sphere to characterize the electrosense capability.
AI.result: Experiments show structured, object-dependent changes in multi-electrode voltage readouts relative to empty-water baselines. Detectability varies across excitation levels (5-20 V) and frequencies (1 mHz to 1 kHz), demonstrating the viability of electrosense for pre-contact sensing.
AI.conclusion: These findings motivate systematic investigation of gripper-integrated electrosense as a complementary pre-contact cue for underwater soft manipulation, addressing the gap in onboard sensing for degraded visibility scenarios.

title: BotDirector: Robot Storytelling Across the Symmetrical Reality with Multi-modal Interactions
summary: Robot storytelling offers a unique blend of technological innovation and creative expression that engages children in unprecedented ways. However, the technical aspects are often too complicated for children. We propose an interactive system that facilitates robot storytelling with tangible and natural language interactions. Children arrange the playground with their own stuff and create narratives with an LLM agent. The created narratives are transformed into a motion sequence based on the map and characters, and the motions are executed by self-navigating swarm robots. This system enhances robot storytelling with flexible scenarios, enabling young children to create robot dramas with everyday objects.

AI.tldr: An interactive system enabling children to create robot stories using everyday objects and natural language, with self-navigating swarm robots bringing the narratives to life.
AI.motivation: Robot storytelling combines technological innovation and creative expression but technical complexity often prevents children from engaging with it.
AI.method: Children arrange a playground with everyday objects (tangible interaction) and create narratives using an LLM agent (natural language interaction). The narratives are transformed into motion sequences based on the map and characters, which are executed by self-navigating swarm robots.
AI.result: The system enables flexible scenarios and allows young children to create robot dramas with everyday objects, enhancing accessibility and engagement in robot storytelling.
AI.conclusion: The system successfully enhances robot storytelling by making it more accessible to young children through intuitive tangible and natural language interactions, enabling creative expression without technical barriers.

title: GeoAlign: Beyond Semantics with State-Guided Spatial Alignment in VLA Models
summary: Current Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models often optimize for semantic grounding, whereas executable manipulation requires geometry-aware spatial alignment and dynamic affordance selection. We introduce GeoAlign, a state-guided spatial alignment architecture for VLA policy learning. GeoAlign post-trains an RGB geometry branch with robot-domain RGB-D supervision, yielding RGB-derived Geometry-Enhanced Post-Trained (GEP) features for policy rollout. The robot's proprioceptive state queries the GEP feature grid, producing compact, phase-dependent geometry tokens for action prediction. GeoAlign achieves 99.0% on LIBERO, 85.3% across three SimplerEnv-Fractal tasks, and 78.8% on eight geometry-critical real-world ALOHA tasks, with ablations confirming the value of geometry post-training and proprioceptive-state-guided querying.

AI.tldr: GeoAlign is a state-guided spatial alignment architecture for VLA policy learning that post-trains an RGB geometry branch with RGB-D supervision, producing geometry-enhanced features queried by proprioceptive state to enable geometry-aware, dynamic affordance selection for robotic manipulation.
