AI.motivation: Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models focus on semantic grounding but lack geometry-aware spatial alignment and dynamic affordance selection, which are essential for executable robotic manipulation tasks.
AI.method: GeoAlign post-trains an RGB geometry branch using robot-domain RGB-D supervision, yielding Geometry-Enhanced Post-Trained (GEP) features. The robot's proprioceptive state queries the GEP feature grid to generate compact, phase-dependent geometry tokens that inform action prediction.
AI.result: GeoAlign achieves 99.0% success on LIBERO, 85.3% across three SimplerEnv-Fractal tasks, and 78.8% on eight geometry-critical real-world ALOHA tasks. Ablation studies confirm the importance of both geometry post-training and proprioceptive-state-guided querying.
AI.conclusion: Integrating geometry-aware spatial alignment with state-guided feature querying into VLA models significantly improves manipulation performance across simulation and real-world benchmarks, demonstrating that geometry post-training and proprioceptive-state-conditioned querying are key design choices for executable robotic policies.

title: AirDreamer: Generalist Drone Navigation with World Models
summary: Navigating a drone in unseen and cluttered environments requires reliable generalization to unseen scene layouts and understanding of environmental structure relative to the robot's capabilities. Previous methods, which assume the same environment configuration, often rely heavily on human-designed perception pipelines and predefined rules to guide the robot toward the target. This process is environment-dependent and generalizes poorly across environments. Inspired by animal navigation behavior, we design a navigation framework that navigates with a reinforcement-learning-based policy on top of a world-model-based environment understanding to overcome these issues. In addition, a sparse reward function without hand-crafted shaping terms is designed to avoid local minima traps and encourage yaw control behaviors. In simulation and on real drones, our method exhibits emergent capabilities for navigating complex, unseen environments and escaping local optima where other methods fail. In challenging maps, it achieves a 5.3% higher navigation success rate than best baseline. Furthermore, the proposed framework achieves effective sim-to-real transfer without any tuning during deployment. The code will be publicly available.

AI.tldr: A drone navigation framework combining a world-model-based environment understanding with a reinforcement-learning policy and a sparse reward function, enabling robust navigation in unseen cluttered environments with effective sim-to-real transfer.
AI.motivation: Existing drone navigation methods rely on environment-dependent human-designed perception pipelines and predefined rules, leading to poor generalization across unseen scene layouts and failure to account for the robot's capabilities relative to environmental structure.
AI.method: The authors propose a navigation framework inspired by animal navigation behavior, consisting of: (1) a world-model-based environment understanding module, (2) a reinforcement-learning-based navigation policy built on top of the world model, and (3) a sparse reward function without hand-crafted shaping terms designed to avoid local minima traps and encourage yaw control behaviors.
AI.result: The method demonstrates emergent capabilities for navigating complex, unseen environments and escaping local optima where baselines fail. It achieves a 5.3% higher navigation success rate than the best baseline on challenging maps and achieves effective sim-to-real transfer on real drones without any tuning during deployment.
AI.conclusion: The proposed world-model-plus-RL framework with sparse rewards enables robust, generalizable drone navigation in unseen cluttered environments, outperforming existing baselines and successfully transferring from simulation to real-world deployment without fine-tuning.

title: Wheel-Mounted/GNSS Fusion with AI-Aided Position Updates
summary: Accurate and robust localization remains a fundamental challenge for autonomous ground vehicles. In this work, we propose a hybrid neural inertial navigation framework that integrates a wheel-mounted inertial sensors, enforced periodic trajectories, and a simple, efficient neural network capable of regressing vehicle displacement with GNSS position updates in an error-state extended Kalman filter. The periodic trajectories increase the inertial signal-to-noise ratio, allowing the network to use only inertial readings to estimate displacement. The approach is validated through real-world experiments using multiple wheel-mounted inertial sensors. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a significant improvement in positioning accuracy, reducing the position root mean squared error by approximately 46 % compared to standard wheel-mounted inertial sensor fusion with GNSS updates.

AI.tldr: A hybrid neural inertial navigation framework combining wheel-mounted inertial sensors, periodic trajectories, and a neural network for displacement regression within an error-state EKF, achieving ~46% reduction in position RMSE over standard sensor fusion with GNSS updates.
AI.motivation: Accurate and robust localization is a fundamental challenge for autonomous ground vehicles, motivating the need for improved inertial navigation methods that can better leverage sensor data for precise positioning.
AI.method: The approach integrates three key components: (1) wheel-mounted inertial sensors, (2) enforced periodic trajectories that increase the inertial signal-to-noise ratio, and (3) a simple, efficient neural network that regresses vehicle displacement using only inertial readings. The neural displacement estimates are fused with GNSS position updates within an error-state extended Kalman filter (EKF) framework.
AI.result: Real-world experiments with multiple wheel-mounted inertial sensors demonstrated that the proposed method significantly improves positioning accuracy, reducing position root mean squared error (RMSE) by approximately 46% compared to standard wheel-mounted inertial sensor fusion with GNSS updates.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid neural inertial navigation framework effectively enhances localization accuracy for autonomous ground vehicles by leveraging periodic trajectories to boost inertial signal quality and a neural network for displacement estimation within an EKF fusion architecture, showing strong potential for practical deployment.

title: EaDex: A Cross-Embodiment Dexterous Manipulation Framework from Low-Cost Demonstrations
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, Conference: CoRL 2026, Submitted as Preprint
summary: Dexterous manipulation learning has long been hindered by the high costs of data and training, as pure reinforcement learning typically requires large-scale interactive exploration and imitation learning depends on high-quality demonstrations that are expensive to collect. To address this problem, we propose EaDex, a multi-embodiment dexterous manipulation learning framework under low-cost demonstration conditions, which enables rapid generation of demonstration data and consequently reduces training time for efficient dexterous manipulation. At the data level, EaDex captures human hand motions using only a single RGB-D camera and constructs structured demonstration data through MANO-based hand modeling, data normalization, and motion retargeting. At the learning level, we introduce a contact-reward-based dynamic demonstration annealing mechanism, which guides early-stage exploration under demonstration and gradually transitions to autonomous optimization with accumulating contact rewards. Using our custom dataset, we evaluate EaDex on three dexterous hands and three articulated object-opening tasks, covering nine cross-embodiment manipulation settings, achieving a 55.3% relative improvement over the baseline without demonstration annealing. These results validate the effectiveness of the proposed low-cost demonstration pipeline and the dynamic demonstration annealing strategy for dexterous manipulation learning.

AI.tldr: EaDex is a multi-embodiment dexterous manipulation learning framework that uses low-cost single RGB-D camera demonstrations with a dynamic demonstration annealing mechanism, achieving 55.3% relative improvement over baselines across nine cross-embodiment settings.
AI.motivation: Dexterous manipulation learning is bottlenecked by the high cost of data and training: reinforcement learning requires large-scale exploration, and imitation learning depends on expensive high-quality demonstrations. The paper aims to reduce these costs while enabling efficient learning across multiple embodiments.
AI.method: EaDex operates at two levels: (1) Data level — captures human hand motions using a single RGB-D camera and constructs structured demonstration data via MANO-based hand modeling, data normalization, and motion retargeting; (2) Learning level — introduces a contact-reward-based dynamic demonstration annealing mechanism that guides early exploration with demonstrations and gradually transitions to autonomous optimization driven by accumulating contact rewards.
AI.result: Evaluated on three dexterous hands and three articulated object-opening tasks across nine cross-embodiment manipulation settings, EaDex achieved a 55.3% relative improvement over the baseline without demonstration annealing, validating both the low-cost demonstration pipeline and the dynamic annealing strategy.
AI.conclusion: The proposed low-cost demonstration pipeline (single RGB-D camera + MANO-based retargeting) combined with the dynamic demonstration annealing mechanism effectively reduces data collection and training costs for dexterous manipulation learning while generalizing across multiple embodiments and tasks.

title: Bridging Predictive Uncertainty and Safe Action: Sample-Conditioned Differentiable Planning for Autonomous Driving
summary: Complex, dynamic, and interactive driving environments pose significant challenges for autonomous driving, primarily due to the pervasive uncertainty of surrounding traffic. A fundamental bottleneck in current systems is the disconnect between highly expressive uncertainty modeling and interpretable, safe motion planning. In this paper, we propose a novel sample-conditioned differentiable planning framework that bridges this gap by explicitly incorporating diffusion-generated future trajectories into the optimization process. Rather than compressing predictions into a single deterministic future or relying on black-box end-to-end architectures, our approach leverages a conditional diffusion model to generate a diverse set of plausible future scenarios. Crucially, these samples are directly fed into a differentiable planner, which explicitly mitigates predictive uncertainty via an empirical Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) tail-risk constraint. This allows the planner to optimize a physically interpretable trajectory that is robust to rare yet safety-critical interactions. Furthermore, we introduce a directed graph representation for scene context that yields substantial improvements in both predictive effectiveness and computational efficiency. Validated through extensive open-loop and closed-loop evaluations on the Waymo Open Motion and Argoverse 2 datasets, our framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in safety, efficiency, and ride comfort.

AI.tldr: A sample-conditioned differentiable planning framework that uses conditional diffusion models to generate diverse future trajectories and employs Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) constraints to optimize safe, interpretable motion planning in autonomous driving.
AI.motivation: Autonomous driving faces significant challenges due to pervasive uncertainty in dynamic environments. Current systems suffer from a disconnect between expressive uncertainty modeling and interpretable, safe motion planning, often relying on deterministic predictions or black-box end-to-end architectures that sacrifice interpretability and safety guarantees.
AI.method: The proposed framework integrates a conditional diffusion model to generate diverse future scenarios, which are directly fed into a differentiable planner. It employs Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) tail-risk constraints to explicitly mitigate predictive uncertainty. Additionally, a directed graph representation for scene context is introduced to enhance predictive effectiveness and computational efficiency.
AI.result: The framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across safety, efficiency, and ride comfort metrics. Extensive open-loop and closed-loop evaluations on Waymo Open Motion and Argoverse 2 datasets demonstrate superior performance in handling complex, dynamic driving scenarios.
AI.conclusion: This approach successfully bridges the gap between uncertainty modeling and safe motion planning, providing a robust, interpretable, and computationally efficient solution for autonomous driving in uncertain environments. The combination of diffusion-based scenario generation with differentiable optimization and CVaR constraints enables safer decision-making in rare, safety-critical interactions.

title: SplitAdapter: Load-Aware Humanoid Loco-Manipulation via Factorized Adaptation
summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires stable whole-body control under varying object masses and pickup/placement heights. This becomes particularly challenging in sim-to-real transfer, where object-induced load variation and robot-side dynamics mismatch interact during physical contact. Existing history-based adapters often compress these factors into a single latent representation, which can weaken robustness under heavy-load manipulation. We propose \textbf{SplitAdapter: Load-Aware Humanoid Loco-Manipulation via Factorized Adaptation}, which freezes a pretrained box manipulation policy and extends it with object/load and dynamics-aware context encoders trained with split world-model objectives, GRL-based cross-adversarial regularization, and hierarchical Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM). In sim-to-sim experiments and real-world deployment, SplitAdapter improves Full-task success over the base policy and world-model FiLM baselines across object masses of $2$, $4$, and $6$ kg and pickup/placement heights of $0$, $30$, and $60$ cm, with the largest improvements under heavy-load conditions.

AI.tldr: SplitAdapter is a factorized adaptation framework for humanoid loco-manipulation that uses separate object/load and dynamics-aware context encoders with split world-model objectives, cross-adversarial regularization, and hierarchical FiLM to improve sim-to-real transfer under varying loads and heights.
AI.motivation: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires stable whole-body control under varying object masses and pickup/placement heights. In sim-to-real transfer, object-induced load variation and robot-side dynamics mismatch interact during physical contact. Existing history-based adapters compress these factors into a single latent representation, weakening robustness under heavy-load manipulation.
AI.method: Freezes a pretrained box manipulation policy and extends it with two factorized context encoders: an object/load-aware encoder and a dynamics-aware encoder. These are trained with split world-model objectives, GRL-based cross-adversarial regularization, and hierarchical Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) to separately model load variation and dynamics mismatch.
AI.result: In sim-to-sim experiments and real-world deployment, SplitAdapter improves Full-task success over the base policy and world-model FiLM baselines across object masses of 2, 4, and 6 kg and pickup/placement heights of 0, 30, and 60 cm, with the largest gains under heavy-load conditions.
AI.conclusion: Factorizing adaptation into load-aware and dynamics-aware components is more effective than single-latent adaptation for sim-to-real humanoid loco-manipulation, especially under heavy loads and varying placement heights.

title: RobotValues: Evaluating Household Robots When Human Values Conflict
summary: While household robots are often evaluated based on task completion, everyday domestic environments involve value-conflicting situations in which robots are expected to choose actions that prioritize other values than task success, such as human autonomy, efficiency, or social appropriateness. Yet, there are no benchmarks for evaluating robots' value preferences in such scenarios. We introduce RobotValues, a benchmark to evaluate household robot planners in 10K value-conflict scenarios. Each instance consists of a realistic household image with multiple plausible robot actions that prioritize different human values. We construct RobotValues through LLM-assisted scenario generation, stakeholder-grounded value extraction, image generation and automatic quality control. Using RobotValues we evaluate VLMs used in robotics and find that models exhibit default value preferences, including safety and accommodation, while underselecting privacy-prioritizing actions. When the models are instructed to prioritize specific values that conflict with their own preferences, they often fail to override their default actions, choosing incorrect actions for 80% of the time. These findings suggest that household robot evaluation should measure not only task completion or safety compliance, but also whether robots can choose among plausible actions when human values conflict.

AI.tldr: RobotValues is a benchmark containing 10K value-conflict scenarios to evaluate household robot planners' value preferences, revealing that VLMs default to safety and accommodation but fail to override these preferences when instructed to prioritize conflicting values.
AI.motivation: Household robots encounter value-conflicting situations requiring prioritization of values like human autonomy, efficiency, or social appropriateness over task success, yet no existing benchmarks exist for evaluating robots' value preferences in such scenarios.
AI.method: RobotValues is constructed through LLM-assisted scenario generation, stakeholder-grounded value extraction, image generation, and automatic quality control, featuring realistic household images with multiple plausible robot actions prioritizing different human values.
AI.result: Evaluations show VLMs exhibit default value preferences (safety and accommodation) while underselecting privacy-prioritizing actions; when instructed to prioritize conflicting values, models fail to override defaults 80% of the time.
AI.conclusion: Household robot evaluation should measure not only task completion or safety compliance but also robots' ability to choose among plausible actions when human values conflict.

title: GPU-Parallel Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning with Demonstration Guided Policy Optimization
summary: Large scale GPU-parallel reinforcement learning has changed what can be trained in robot simulation, yet most systems still optimize one specialist policy per task. We propose a construction methodology for turning structured manipulation task families into GPU-parallel multi-task RL benchmarks, and instantiate it as MT-Libero using LIBERO assets and task predicates in Isaac Lab. The resulting benchmark supports simultaneous reinforcement learning over heterogeneous task suites with parallel rendering, physics randomization, and state-input or visual-input policies. To make such training practical under sparse success signals and limited prior data, we further propose DGPO, an on-policy demonstration guided method that combines importance weighted PPO with adaptive behavior cloning on matched demonstration actions. DGPO enables a tunable preference toward demonstrated task distributions, outperforming both prior-free RL and existing demonstration-based methods while preserving the stability and online improvement benefits of on-policy PPO.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a methodology for constructing GPU-parallel multi-task RL benchmarks (instantiated as MT-Libero) and introduces DGPO, a demonstration-guided on-policy RL method that combines importance-weighted PPO with adaptive behavior cloning to enable practical multi-task training under sparse rewards.
AI.motivation: Existing large-scale GPU-parallel RL systems for robot simulation still optimize one specialist policy per task. There is a lack of structured multi-task benchmarks and effective training methods that can handle heterogeneous task suites simultaneously, especially under sparse success signals and limited prior demonstration data.
AI.method: Two contributions: (1) A construction methodology for GPU-parallel multi-task RL benchmarks, instantiated as MT-Libero using LIBERO assets and predicates in Isaac Lab, supporting parallel rendering, physics randomization, and both state-input and visual-input policies. (2) DGPO, an on-policy demonstration-guided RL algorithm that integrates importance-weighted PPO with adaptive behavior cloning on matched demonstration actions, providing a tunable preference toward demonstrated task distributions.
AI.result: DGPO outperforms both prior-free RL and existing demonstration-based methods, while preserving the stability and online improvement benefits of on-policy PPO. MT-Libero successfully supports simultaneous RL across heterogeneous task suites with parallel rendering and physics randomization.
AI.conclusion: Structured multi-task GPU-parallel RL benchmarks can be systematically constructed, and demonstration-guided on-policy methods like DGPO can make simultaneous multi-task training practical even under sparse rewards and limited prior data, bridging the gap between single-task specialist policies and generalist multi-task learning.

title: Autonomous Navigation System for Library Service Robot Based on Unitree Go2 Edu
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Accepted by WCCIS 2026
summary: Libraries require autonomous robots to move quietly through narrow aisles while remaining safe around readers, chairs, bags, and carts. This paper presents a ROS 2 navigation system for a Unitree Go2 Edu quadruped equipped with a 4D LiDAR, a front depth camera, and an IMU. Rather than assuming the library is rough terrain, we target the practical mobility discontinuities of real deployments, including floor transitions, temporary clutter, and partially blocked passages where low-clearance wheeled platforms are less tolerant. RTAB-Map is used for visual-LiDAR SLAM, AMCL and EKF-based sensor fusion provide localization, and a Nav2 stack with A* and DWA supports planning and local avoidance. In a real library, the system achieves 100%, 96%, and 88% success rates in static, low-density dynamic, and high-density dynamic scenes, while map validation against surveyed control distances yields a mean metric error of 3.7 cm.

AI.tldr: A ROS 2 navigation system for a Unitree Go2 Edu quadruped equipped with 4D LiDAR, depth camera, and IMU that achieves high success rates (88-100%) in real library environments by addressing practical mobility discontinuities through visual-LiDAR SLAM, sensor fusion, and adaptive planning.
AI.motivation: Libraries require autonomous robots to move quietly through narrow aisles while maintaining safety around readers, furniture, and obstacles. Existing solutions often assume idealized environments rather than addressing real-world challenges like floor transitions, temporary clutter, and partially blocked passages that pose difficulties for wheeled platforms.
AI.method: The system uses RTAB-Map for visual-LiDAR SLAM, AMCL and EKF-based sensor fusion for localization, and Nav2 stack with A* and DWA for planning and local avoidance. The robot is equipped with a Unitree Go2 Edu quadruped, 4D LiDAR, front depth camera, and IMU. The approach specifically targets practical mobility discontinuities including floor transitions, temporary clutter, and partially blocked passages.
AI.result: In real library tests, the system achieved 100% success rate in static scenes, 96% in low-density dynamic scenes, and 88% in high-density dynamic scenes. Map validation against surveyed control distances yielded a mean metric error of 3.7 cm, demonstrating high precision.
AI.conclusion: The proposed navigation system effectively addresses real-world library navigation challenges by handling mobility discontinuities and dynamic environments, achieving near-perfect success rates in controlled conditions and maintaining high accuracy in dynamic settings. This demonstrates the viability of quadruped robots for practical library service applications.

title: eMEM: A Hybrid Spatio-Temporal Memory System For Embodied Agents
summary: We present eMEM (Embodied Memory), a hybrid graph-based memory system for embodied agents operating in physical environments. Current agent memory architectures, such as Generative Agents, MemGPT, and A-MEM, treat memory as text streams or knowledge graphs, but embodied agents require memory that is simultaneously searchable by meaning, space, and time. eMEM fills this gap with a multi-index architecture (SQL ITE for structured storage, hnswlib for approximate nearest neighbour semantic search, and an R-tree for spatial queries) unified behind a single graph model. A tiered consolidation pipeline transforms raw perceptual observations into compressed summaries, mirroring hippocampal-neocortical consolidation in biological systems. Ten agent-facing recall tools expose memory retrieval primitives, including concept-to-location resolution and cross layer recall, as first-class operations for LLM tool calling. The system is fully embedded and runs in-process alongside the agent. In addition we introduce eMEM-Bench v1, a benchmark we construct over ProcTHOR-10K scenes for embodied memory evaluation. The benchmark is organised explicitly around eight cognitive-psychology paradigms (DRM lures, pattern separation, pattern completion, source monitoring, context-dependent retrieval, long-horizon interference, serial position, and a foil augmented retention curve), each chosen so that the result is interpretable against the broader memory-systems literature in humans and prior agent-memory systems; a level of diagnostic that surface-task benchmarks like LoCoMo or OpenEQA cannot provide. eMEM scores 80.8 weighted mean over 988 probes, with a flat retention curve at ceiling from 1 h to 1 yr of simulated delay on room-unique items. We show that a pure RAG baseline (the flat_rag ablation) loses 30 pt on context dependent retrieval and 29 pt on DRM lure rejection, isolating the contribution of multi-layer storage and consolidation respectively. We release both the system and the benchmark code.

AI.tldr: eMEM is a hybrid graph-based memory system for embodied agents that integrates structured storage, semantic search, and spatial queries through a multi-index architecture with a hippocampal-inspired consolidation pipeline, achieving superior performance on a novel benchmark designed around cognitive-psychology paradigms.
AI.motivation: Existing agent memory architectures (Generative Agents, MemGPT, A-MEM) treat memory as text streams or knowledge graphs, but embodied agents require memory that is simultaneously searchable by meaning, space, and time.
AI.method: eMEM uses a multi-index architecture combining SQL ITE for structured storage, hnswlib for approximate nearest neighbour semantic search, and an R-tree for spatial queries, unified behind a single graph model. A tiered consolidation pipeline transforms raw observations into compressed summaries. Ten agent-facing recall tools expose memory retrieval primitives including concept-to-location resolution and cross layer recall.
AI.result: eMEM achieves 80.8 weighted mean on eMEM-Bench v1 over 988 probes, with flat retention curve at ceiling from 1 hour to 1 year on room-unique items. A pure RAG baseline loses 30 points on context-dependent retrieval and 29 points on DRM lure rejection.
AI.conclusion: The multi-layer storage and consolidation mechanisms significantly contribute to performance, demonstrating that embodied agents need memory systems that integrate multiple dimensions (meaning, space, time) rather than treating memory as simple text streams or knowledge graphs. The benchmark provides diagnostic capability that surface-task benchmarks cannot.

title: Grasp-Then-Plan with Failure Attribution: A Closed Two-Stage Framework for Precise and Generalizable Robotic Manipulation
summary: In robotic manipulation, the tight coupling between grasping and motion planning often obscures the true source of failure, leading to inefficient trial-and-error. To enable efficient long-horizon manipulation, we propose GTP-FA (Grasp-Then-Plan with Failure Attribution), a task-oriented two-stage grasp-then-plan framework that generates grasp candidates and performs downstream motion planning conditioned on the selected grasp. Given a failed manipulation trajectory, we learn a failure attribution model that generalizes to unseen grasps and produces a stable distribution over failure modes for diagnosis-guided optimization. Based on these attribution results, we then optimize both modules in a diagnosis-driven manner: on the grasping side, we inject task-level priors and risk penalties into grasp candidate scoring and optimization to suppress unstable or task-incompatible grasps; on the planning side, we target high-risk initial states through data collection and fine-tuning to address genuine planning bottlenecks. We evaluate the proposed framework in both simulation and real-robot experiments, and show that GTP-FA improves the corresponding base learners across RL, IL, diffusion-policy, and VLA-based settings, achieving substantially higher overall task success rates.

AI.tldr: GTP-FA is a two-stage grasp-then-plan framework with a learned failure attribution model that diagnoses manipulation failures and guides targeted optimization of both grasping and motion planning modules, improving success rates across RL, IL, diffusion-policy, and VLA settings in simulation and real-robot experiments.
AI.motivation: In robotic manipulation, grasping and motion planning are tightly coupled, making it difficult to identify the true source of failure. This ambiguity leads to inefficient trial-and-error, especially in long-horizon tasks where repeated failures without diagnosis waste resources and hinder learning.
AI.method: The authors propose GTP-FA, a task-oriented two-stage grasp-then-plan framework. It first generates grasp candidates and performs motion planning conditioned on the selected grasp. A learned failure attribution model analyzes failed trajectories, generalizing to unseen grasps and producing a stable distribution over failure modes. Based on attribution results, two modules are optimized: (1) on the grasping side, task-level priors and risk penalties are injected into grasp scoring to suppress unstable or task-incompatible grasps; (2) on the planning side, targeted data collection and fine-tuning address high-risk initial states to resolve genuine planning bottlenecks.
AI.result: GTP-FA was evaluated in both simulation and real-robot experiments. It consistently improves base learners across diverse settings including RL, IL, diffusion-policy, and VLA-based methods, achieving substantially higher overall task success rates compared to baselines without failure attribution.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling failure attribution in tightly coupled grasp-and-plan pipelines enables diagnosis-driven, targeted optimization of each module. GTP-FA demonstrates that identifying and addressing the true source of manipulation failures—rather than blindly retrying—leads to more efficient and effective long-horizon robotic manipulation across a broad range of learning paradigms.

title: Extreme Motion Generation via Hybrid Null-Space Control for Straight-Line Path Following
summary: This work studies ``extreme motion generation'', which aims to maximize the Cartesian path length along a pre-defined trajectory within the manipulator's workspace. This objective is important in industry as long as path-following is fundamental to a large variety of tasks such as surface coating and welding. More critically, extreme motion enables a fixed-base manipulator to exploit the kinematic capability under limited reachability. However, such exploitation is challenging in practice, as the manipulator must actively avoid the safety boundary through execution, which is inherently a long-horizon problem. Accordingly, we claim that long-horizon decision-making should be delegated to a learning-based policy to maximize exploitation, while a classical model-based controller covers the near-boundary region, where the learning policy degrades sharply due to sparse data coverage. In detail, our proposed method is a step-level hybrid controller that switches between an RL-based and a model-based controller according to the normalized joint-limit distance. The initial joint configuration is sampled through conditional diffusion-based sampling, which improves the achievable path length based on the learned motion prior. We evaluate the proposed framework on 10,000 straight-line path-following tasks with a 7-DoF Franka FR3, extending the average rollout length by 27\% over the model-based baseline. Notably, certain tasks yield a pronounced extension toward the motion extreme, as reflected in the maximum improvement reported in the statistical results. The project website and related videos of this paper can be found at https://yuan-xinyi.github.io/extreme-motion-generation/.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hybrid RL + model-based controller with diffusion-based initial configuration sampling to maximize Cartesian path-following length for fixed-base manipulators, achieving 27% average improvement over model-based baselines on a 7-DoF Franka FR3.
AI.motivation: Maximizing Cartesian path length along pre-defined trajectories (extreme motion generation) is critical for industrial tasks such as surface coating and welding, especially under limited reachability of fixed-base manipulators. However, actively avoiding safety boundaries during execution makes this a challenging long-horizon decision-making problem.
AI.method: A step-level hybrid controller that switches between an RL-based policy and a classical model-based controller based on the normalized joint-limit distance. Long-horizon decisions are delegated to the RL policy for maximal exploitation, while the model-based controller handles near-boundary regions where the RL policy degrades due to sparse data. Additionally, initial joint configurations are sampled via conditional diffusion-based sampling to leverage learned motion priors and improve achievable path length.
AI.result: Evaluated on 10,000 straight-line path-following tasks with a 7-DoF Franka FR3 robot. The proposed framework extends the average rollout length by 27% over the model-based baseline, with some tasks showing pronounced extension toward motion extremes.
AI.conclusion: Combining learning-based (RL + diffusion) and model-based approaches in a hybrid framework effectively addresses the long-horizon extreme motion generation problem for manipulators, significantly extending path-following capabilities beyond what classical controllers alone can achieve.

title: OpenEAI-Platform: An Open-source Embodied Artificial Intelligence Hardware-Software Unified Platform
summary: Embodied AI in the real world requires both accurate hardware and robust vision-language-action (VLA) policies. We present OpenEAI-Platform, a fully open-source platform that integrates a low-cost 6+1 degree-of-freedom (dof) robotic arm (OpenEAI-Arm) and a reproducible VLA model (OpenEAI-VLA). OpenEAI-Arm provides open-source mechanical designs for low manufacturing cost and compliant control methods for higher accuracy. OpenEAI-VLA builds on Qwen3-VL-4B and uses a Diffusion Transformer action head, and is trained in two stages with only open-source robot and multimodal datasets. Across four real-world manipulation tasks, OpenEAI-Arm outperforms two commercial 6+1-dof arms under the same policy, and OpenEAI-VLA achieves success rates comparable to the large-scale pretrained pi0 baseline with only limited pretraining data. We will release the full hardware designs, drivers, models, and training/data pipelines to support reproducible research and scalable data collection. Our codes, layouts, and models will be released after the paper is accepted.

AI.tldr: OpenEAI-Platform is a fully open-source embodied AI platform combining a low-cost 6+1-DOF robotic arm (OpenEAI-Arm) with a reproducible vision-language-action model (OpenEAI-VLA), demonstrating competitive real-world manipulation performance against both commercial hardware and large-scale pretrained baselines.
AI.motivation: Embodied AI deployed in the real world demands both accurate, affordable hardware and robust vision-language-action (VLA) policies. Existing solutions often rely on expensive commercial arms or closed-source models, limiting reproducibility and scalable data collection for the research community.
AI.method: The platform integrates two components: (1) OpenEAI-Arm — a low-cost 6+1-DOF robotic arm with open-source mechanical designs and compliant control for higher accuracy; (2) OpenEAI-VLA — a VLA model built on Qwen3-VL-4B with a Diffusion Transformer action head, trained in two stages using only open-source robot and multimodal datasets. Full hardware designs, drivers, models, and training/data pipelines are to be released.
AI.result: Across four real-world manipulation tasks, OpenEAI-Arm outperformed two commercial 6+1-DOF arms under the same policy, and OpenEAI-VLA achieved success rates comparable to the large-scale pretrained pi0 baseline while using only limited pretraining data.
AI.conclusion: OpenEAI-Platform demonstrates that a fully open-source, low-cost embodied AI system can match or exceed commercial and large-scale alternatives in real-world manipulation, thereby enabling reproducible research and scalable data collection for the broader community.

title: Reliability-Guided Depth Fusion for Glare-Resilient Navigation Costmaps
summary: Specular glare on reflective floors, glass boundaries, and glossy indoor surfaces frequently corrupts active-stereo RGB-D depth measurements, producing holes and spikes that accumulate as persistent phantom obstacles in occupancy-grid costmaps. This paper presents a glare-resilient costmap construction method based on explicit depth-reliability modeling. A lightweight Depth Reliability Map network (DRM-Net) predicts per-pixel measurement trustworthiness under specular interference, and a reliability-guided weighted-and-gated fusion (RGF) mechanism modulates occupancy updates before corrupted measurements are accumulated into the map. To support robust training and evaluation, the method uses pose-aligned multi-view reference-depth construction to reduce circular-supervision bias and is evaluated through fusion-variant ablations, parameter-sensitivity analysis, cross-condition tests, paired navigation comparisons, reliability-map metrics, and embedded runtime profiling. Experiments on a real mobile robotic platform equipped with an Intel RealSense D435 and a Jetson Orin Nano show that the proposed method reduces false obstacle insertion, improves free-space preservation, and maintains real-time throughput under reflective-floor, glass-wall, and natural-light glare conditions. These results support treating glare as a measurement-reliability problem rather than as a dense depth-completion problem for safety-critical indoor navigation.

AI.tldr: A glare-resilient costmap construction method using a Depth Reliability Map network (DRM-Net) to predict measurement trustworthiness and a reliability-guided weighted-and-gated fusion (RGF) mechanism to modulate occupancy updates under specular glare conditions.
AI.motivation: Specular glare on reflective surfaces corrupts active-stereo RGB-D depth measurements, producing holes and spikes that accumulate as persistent phantom obstacles in occupancy-grid costmaps, threatening safety-critical indoor navigation.
AI.method: A lightweight Depth Reliability Map network (DRM-Net) predicts per-pixel measurement trustworthiness under specular interference, and a reliability-guided weighted-and-gated fusion (RGF) mechanism modulates occupancy updates before corrupted measurements are accumulated into the map. The method uses pose-aligned multi-view reference-depth construction to reduce circular-supervision bias and is evaluated through fusion-variant ablations, parameter-sensitivity analysis, cross-condition tests, paired navigation comparisons, reliability-map metrics, and runtime profiling.
AI.result: Experiments on a mobile robot with Intel RealSense D435 and Jetson Orin Nano demonstrate that the proposed method reduces false obstacle insertion, improves free-space preservation, and maintains real-time throughput under reflective-floor, glass-wall, and natural-light glare conditions.
AI.conclusion: The results support treating glare as a measurement-reliability problem rather than as a dense depth-completion problem for safety-critical indoor navigation.

title: PerchRL: Vision-Based Agile Perching on Inclined Platforms under Rapid and Irregular Motion
summary: Autonomous vision-based perching of quadrotors on moving inclined platforms is critical for air-ground collaboration but remains challenging due to the limited field of view (FOV). In this paper, we propose PerchRL, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework for vision-based agile perching on inclined platforms under rapid and irregular motion. Specifically, we employ a two-stage learning strategy consisting of state-based pre-training followed by vision-based fine-tuning. To improve generalization across diverse platform motions, we employ randomized platform trajectories to prevent overfitting and temporal augmentation methods to capture latent motion patterns from historical observations. During vision-based fine-tuning, a hybrid learning framework consisting of visibility-aware state augmentation and active perception rewards is presented to improve robustness under intermittent visual loss. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate the feasibility, stability, and real-time performance of PerchRL, while successful deployment across distinct quadrotor platforms further validates its adaptability. The source code will be released to benefit the community.

AI.tldr: PerchRL is a reinforcement learning framework enabling quadrotors to autonomously perch on moving inclined platforms using vision, addressing limited FOV challenges through a two-stage learning strategy (state-based pre-training + vision-based fine-tuning) with domain randomization and hybrid learning techniques for robustness against visual loss.
AI.motivation: Autonomous vision-based perching of quadrotors on moving inclined platforms is essential for air-ground collaboration but is challenging due to the limited field of view (FOV), rapid and irregular platform motion, and intermittent visual loss. Existing methods struggle with generalization and robustness under these conditions.
AI.method: A two-stage RL learning strategy: (1) state-based pre-training with randomized platform trajectories to prevent overfitting and temporal augmentation to capture latent motion patterns from historical observations; (2) vision-based fine-tuning using a hybrid learning framework that combines visibility-aware state augmentation and active perception rewards to handle intermittent visual loss robustly.
AI.result: Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate the feasibility, stability, and real-time performance of PerchRL. Successful deployment across distinct quadrotor platforms further validates the framework's adaptability and generalization capability.
AI.conclusion: PerchRL effectively addresses the challenges of vision-based perching on moving inclined platforms by combining domain randomization, temporal augmentation, and a hybrid vision-based fine-tuning strategy, achieving robust and generalizable perching across diverse conditions and hardware platforms.

title: Human2Humanoid: Physics-Aware Cross-Morphology Motion Retargeting for Humanoid Robots
summary: Retargeting human motion to humanoid robots is critical for teleoperation, imitation learning and human-robot interaction. However, it remains challenging because of substantial morphological discrepancies between humans and robots, including differences in skeletal topology, limb proportions and degrees of freedom, as well as the scarcity of paired motion data. This paper presents Human2Humanoid, an unsupervised motion retargeting framework that transfers human motions to humanoid robot behaviors with high fidelity. To bridge the domain gap under unpaired data, we adopt a CycleGAN-based architecture equipped with a skeleton-aware graph convolutional network to capture topology-dependent motion features. To address cross-domain scale mismatches, we introduce a morphology-invariant end-effector consistency loss that aligns normalized end-effector trajectories to preserve motion semantics across embodiments. To improve physical plausibility and reduce contact artifacts, we impose explicit physics-aware feasibility constraints to encourage reproduction of the contact patterns in the source motion. Experimental results show that the proposed method successfully retargets human motion to the Unitree G1 humanoid robot without paired data, and outperforms existing methods in both downstream controllability and physical feasibility.

AI.tldr: Human2Humanoid is an unsupervised motion retargeting framework that transfers human motions to humanoid robots with high fidelity using a CycleGAN-based architecture with skeleton-aware graph convolutional networks, morphology-invariant end-effector consistency losses, and physics-aware feasibility constraints to bridge morphological discrepancies and scale mismatches without paired data.
AI.motivation: Motion retargeting from humans to humanoid robots is essential for teleoperation, imitation learning, and human-robot interaction. However, it remains challenging due to substantial morphological discrepancies (skeletal topology, limb proportions, degrees of freedom) and the scarcity of paired motion data between humans and robots.
AI.method: The framework employs a CycleGAN-based architecture enhanced with a skeleton-aware graph convolutional network (SGCN) to capture topology-dependent motion features. It introduces a morphology-invariant end-effector consistency loss to align normalized end-effector trajectories, preserving motion semantics across embodiments. Additionally, physics-aware feasibility constraints are imposed to encourage reproduction of contact patterns, improving physical plausibility and reducing contact artifacts.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate successful retargeting of human motion to the Unitree G1 humanoid robot without paired data. The proposed method outperforms existing approaches in both downstream controllability and physical feasibility metrics.
AI.conclusion: Human2Humanoid effectively bridges the domain gap between human and robot morphologies through unsupervised learning, achieving high-fidelity motion retargeting that addresses cross-domain scale mismatches and contact artifacts while maintaining physical plausibility.

title: SPADE: Sketch-guided Path Planning Augmented with Diffusion Experts
summary: Path planning is essential for Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs). Conventional methods for incorporating human preferences into planning typically rely on either complex reward engineering or hardware-intensive solutions. Recent state-of-the-art frameworks leverage imitation learning to train behavior-specific path planning models from expert demonstrations. However, these approaches face two key limitations: limited generalization to unseen environments and low robustness in demonstration collection. To address these challenges, this work introduces an enhanced framework that focuses on two main contributions: an overhauled annotation tool built on ROS 2, and a novel training strategy that integrates diffusion-based augmentation into baseline behavioral cloning models. A dataset of expert demonstrations is provided and evaluated through ablation studies to assess the robustness of the proposed solution. The enhanced approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods with 39.1% lower Absolute Pose Error (APE) and 33.5% lower Fr'echet Inception Distance (FID) while having 93.8% less trainable parameters. Moreover it attains diffusion-level generalization while preserving the real-time, on-edge properties of state-of-the-art models.

AI.tldr: An enhanced imitation learning framework for AMR path planning that combines a ROS 2-based annotation tool with diffusion-based augmentation for behavioral cloning, achieving better generalization and lower error than state-of-the-art methods with significantly fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing imitation learning approaches for incorporating human preferences into AMR path planning suffer from limited generalization to unseen environments and low robustness in demonstration collection, while conventional methods rely on complex reward engineering or hardware-intensive solutions.
AI.method: The paper introduces two main contributions: (1) an overhauled annotation tool built on ROS 2 for robust demonstration collection, and (2) a novel training strategy that integrates diffusion-based augmentation into baseline behavioral cloning models. An expert demonstration dataset is constructed and evaluated via ablation studies.
AI.result: The proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods with 39.1% lower Absolute Pose Error (APE), 33.5% lower Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), and 93.8% fewer trainable parameters, while achieving diffusion-level generalization and maintaining real-time, on-edge inference capability.
AI.conclusion: The enhanced framework successfully addresses the generalization and robustness limitations of existing imitation learning methods for AMR path planning, offering a lightweight yet high-performing solution that combines diffusion-level generalization with real-time deployability on edge devices.

title: Bionic Human-Motion Style Transfer for Physically Executable Whole-Body Control of Humanoid Robots
summary: Expressive whole-body motion is important for humanoid robots operating in human environments, where robots are expected to move stably while presenting readable and adjustable body behaviors. However, most expressive motions are still obtained from fixed demonstrations or manually designed scripts, making it difficult to reuse a demonstrated style across different motion contents. Inspired by the way human motion styles convey affective and intentional cues through gait rhythm, posture, arm swing and body sway, this paper proposes a bionic generation-to-control framework for exemplar-driven style transfer on humanoid robots. Given a short human style exemplar and a target content motion, the proposed framework generates a stylized whole-body reference that preserves the intended motion content while transferring the demonstrated style. A physics-aware multi-condition latent diffusion model is developed to fuse style, content and trajectory conditions, and classifier-free guidance is used to adjust the style intensity without retraining. To improve hardware executability, contact-consistency and temporal-smoothness regularization are imposed on decoded motions during training. The generated references are then converted into G1-compatible robot references and executed by a preview-based whole-body tracking policy trained with a cluster-and-distill strategy. Simulation and Unitree G1 experiments show that the proposed method can transfer short human style exemplars to diverse robot motion contents, reduce contact and jitter artifacts compared with animation-oriented style-transfer baselines, and achieve a 96.0% success rate over 125 reported real-robot trials. The results demonstrate the feasibility of using short human motion exemplars as reusable bionic sources for physically executable expressive humanoid motion.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a bionic generation-to-control framework for exemplar-driven style transfer on humanoid robots, using a physics-aware latent diffusion model to generate stylized whole-body motions from short human style exemplars and execute them on the Unitree G1 robot with a 96.0% success rate over 125 real-robot trials.
AI.motivation: Expressive whole-body motion is essential for humanoid robots in human environments, but current approaches rely on fixed demonstrations or manually designed scripts, making it difficult to reuse a demonstrated motion style across different motion contents. The paper aims to enable reusable, physically executable style transfer from short human motion exemplars to diverse robot motions.
AI.method: A physics-aware multi-condition latent diffusion model fuses style, content, and trajectory conditions to generate stylized whole-body references. Classifier-free guidance adjusts style intensity without retraining. Contact-consistency and temporal-smoothness regularization are imposed during training to improve hardware executability. Generated references are converted to G1-compatible robot references and executed via a preview-based whole-body tracking policy trained with a cluster-and-distill strategy.
AI.result: Simulation and Unitree G1 experiments demonstrate that the method transfers short human style exemplars to diverse robot motion contents, reduces contact and jitter artifacts compared to animation-oriented baselines, and achieves a 96.0% success rate across 125 real-robot trials.
AI.conclusion: Short human motion exemplars can serve as reusable bionic sources for generating physically executable expressive whole-body motions on humanoid robots, bridging the gap between stylistic motion generation and real-world hardware deployment.

title: Static and Dynamic Representations for Tactile Contact-Angle Estimation with Event-Based Sensors
comment: 8 pages, 8 figures. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RAL), under review
summary: Event-based tactile sensing offers low-latency signal acquisition for contact-rich robotic interaction. This paper investigates contact-angle estimation using event streams from an event-based tactile sensor (NeuroTac) and compares three event-derived spatial contour representations: a dynamic representation capturing recent event activity, a static representation recovering a more persistent contact state, and their combined representation. Across the evaluated motion scenarios, all representation pipelines exhibited P99 processing latency below 10 ms at all tested sampling intervals, demonstrating their potential for high-frequency event-based tactile angle estimation in robotic manipulation. The static representation consistently achieved marginally better performance than the dynamic and combined representations under scenario-specific training, yielding a mean overall MAE of 0.160° during continuous sensor rolling and a stop-phase mean MAE of 0.251° during randomly inserted motion interruptions. It also exhibited smaller performance fluctuations across speed and indentation depth variations than the other two representations.

AI.tldr: This paper compares three event-derived spatial contour representations (dynamic, static, and combined) from an event-based tactile sensor (NeuroTac) for contact-angle estimation, finding that all achieve sub-10 ms P99 latency while the static representation yields the best accuracy and robustness across varying motion conditions.
AI.motivation: Event-based tactile sensing enables low-latency signal acquisition for contact-rich robotic interaction, but effective spatial contour representations from event streams for contact-angle estimation remain underexplored. A systematic comparison of different event-derived representations is needed to identify the most accurate and robust approach for high-frequency tactile estimation in robotic manipulation.
AI.method: The authors use the NeuroTac event-based tactile sensor to generate event streams and evaluate three spatial contour representations: (1) a dynamic representation capturing recent event activity, (2) a static representation recovering a more persistent contact state, and (3) a combined representation fusing both. These representations are tested under multiple motion scenarios including continuous sensor rolling and randomly inserted motion interruptions, with evaluations across varying speeds, indentation depths, and sampling intervals.
AI.result: All three representation pipelines achieved P99 processing latency below 10 ms at all tested sampling intervals. Under scenario-specific training, the static representation consistently outperformed the dynamic and combined representations, achieving a mean overall MAE of 0.160° during continuous rolling and a stop-phase mean MAE of 0.251° during motion interruptions. The static representation also showed smaller performance fluctuations across speed and indentation depth variations.
AI.conclusion: Event-based tactile sensing with appropriate spatial contour representations is viable for high-frequency, low-latency contact-angle estimation in robotic manipulation. Among the three evaluated representations, the static representation provides the best balance of accuracy, robustness, and latency, making it a strong candidate for real-time tactile feedback in contact-rich robotic tasks.

title: NVIDIA Isaac Sim: Enabling Scalable, GPU-Accelerated Simulation for Robotics
summary: Simulation has become a core infrastructure for robotics research. Unlike previous simulators, NVIDIA Isaac Sim leverages GPU acceleration to enable large-scale parallel training and physics-accurate modeling. Its synthetic data generation pipeline alleviates the scarcity of high-quality training data, supporting data-driven robot learning and large-scale simulation-centric experimentation. However, existing surveys often treat it as one simulator among many, without a systematic analysis of its architectural characteristics, usage patterns, and limitations. This survey reviews Isaac Sim from system and application perspectives, outlining its architecture and comparing it with widely used simulators. We analyze representative studies across five major domains and summarize common usage patterns, particularly in data generation and high-fidelity simulation. We also outline key future directions and challenges, including physics open-world learning, simulation-centric training and practical usability constraints.

AI.tldr: A systematic survey analyzing NVIDIA Isaac Sim's GPU-accelerated architecture, usage patterns, and limitations across five major robotics domains, while identifying future challenges in physics open-world learning and simulation-centric training.
AI.motivation: Simulation is essential for robotics research, but existing surveys inadequately analyze Isaac Sim's unique GPU acceleration capabilities, synthetic data generation pipeline, and architectural characteristics. The scarcity of systematic reviews prevents researchers from fully understanding its potential and limitations.
AI.method: The survey adopts a dual perspective (system and application) to review Isaac Sim, comparing its architecture with other simulators, analyzing representative studies across five major domains, and summarizing common usage patterns with emphasis on data generation and high-fidelity simulation.
AI.result: The review provides a comprehensive analysis of Isaac Sim's architecture and usage patterns, identifies common approaches in data generation and high-fidelity simulation, and categorizes future directions including physics open-world learning, simulation-centric training, and practical usability constraints.
AI.conclusion: This survey fills a critical gap in the literature by providing the first systematic analysis of Isaac Sim's unique contributions to robotics research, establishing a foundation for understanding its capabilities, limitations, and future research directions in simulation-centric robot learning.

title: Partially Observable Adversarial Patch Attacks on Vision-Language-Action Models in Robotics
comment: Accepted by IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters, 2026
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are gaining attention in robotics, yet their robustness to adversarial attacks remains largely unexplored. Existing work shows that adversarial patches can mislead VLA-based robots but assumes full access to the entire execution trajectory, an unrealistic requirement in practice. We address this limitation by formulating a partially observable threat model, where the adversary can exploit only a short prefix of the trajectory to generate a fixed patch applied to all subsequent frames. Under this setting, we propose a two-phase framework. First, we localize the patch using the model's attention maps to identify visually critical regions that correspond to the full instruction. Then, we optimize the patch to disrupt the semantic grounding of target objects and increase the curvature of action trajectories, thereby compounding failures in both perception and control. Extensive experiments in simulation and real-world robotic environments show that our method sustains adversarial effects under partial observability, inducing long-horizon disruptions and significantly reducing task success rates.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a two-phase adversarial attack framework against vision-language-action (VLA) models in robotics under a realistic partially observable threat model, where the adversary only accesses a short prefix of the execution trajectory. The method localizes critical regions via attention maps and optimizes adversarial patches to disrupt both perception and control, achieving sustained long-horizon disruptions in simulation and real-world experiments.
AI.motivation: While VLA models are increasingly deployed in robotics, their adversarial robustness is largely unexplored. Existing adversarial patch attacks on VLA-based robots assume full access to the entire execution trajectory, which is unrealistic in practice. There is a need to study adversarial vulnerabilities under more practical, partially observable conditions.
AI.method: A two-phase framework under a partially observable threat model (adversary sees only a short trajectory prefix to generate a fixed patch for all subsequent frames): (1) Patch localization using the model's attention maps to identify visually critical regions corresponding to the full instruction; (2) Patch optimization to disrupt semantic grounding of target objects and increase action trajectory curvature, compounding failures in both perception and control.
AI.result: Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world robotic environments demonstrate that the proposed method sustains adversarial effects under partial observability, induces long-horizon disruptions, and significantly reduces task success rates of VLA-based robotic systems.
AI.conclusion: Adversarial patches can effectively attack VLA-based robots even under realistic partial observability constraints, posing a serious security concern. The proposed attention-guided localization and dual-objective (perception + control) optimization framework demonstrates that compounded perception-and-control failures can be achieved with only limited trajectory access.

title: CANMOT: Class-Aware Noise Modeling for Multi-Object Tracking in Autonomous Driving
comment: submitted to IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary:
Kalman filter (KF)-based multi-object tracking (MOT) remains a strong baseline for autonomous driving due to its strong performance, computational efficiency and interpretability. In most practical systems, the process noise and measurement noise covariances are defined globally and shared across object classes, presuming identical uncertainty characteristics across heterogeneous traffic participants.
  This work revisits this assumption and proposes CANMOT, a class-aware and object-aligned noise modeling framework for KF-based 3D MOT. Class-specific diagonal process and measurement covariance matrices are introduced and optionally expressed in the object coordinate frame to preserve longitudinal-lateral anisotropy.
  Systematic experiments on the nuScenes benchmark show that class-aware and object-aligned noise modeling improves tracking performance and substantially reduces identity switches compared to state-of-the-art (SotA). In addition, the consistency of the estimated uncertainty is analyzed using the Average Normalized Estimation Error Squared (ANEES) and $χ^2$-based violation tests. The results reveal severe overconfidence in standard KF-based MOT baselines. While the proposed formulation improves calibration without modifying the underlying filtering framework, it still exhibits substantial inconsistency, highlighting the need for further research in this area.
  Code is available at https://github.com/rst-tu-dortmund/learned-3d-nms.

AI.tldr: CANMOT proposes class-aware and object-aligned noise modeling for KF-based 3D MOT in autonomous driving, improving tracking performance and reducing identity switches compared to standard KF baselines.
AI.motivation: Standard KF-based MOT assumes globally shared noise covariances across all object classes, which doesn't reflect the real-world heterogeneity of traffic participants with different uncertainty characteristics.
AI.method: Introduces class-specific diagonal process and measurement covariance matrices, optionally expressed in object coordinate frame to preserve longitudinal-lateral anisotropy, while maintaining the underlying KF framework.
AI.result: Experiments on nuScenes benchmark show improved tracking performance and reduced identity switches. Analysis reveals severe overconfidence in standard KF baselines, though the proposed method still exhibits substantial inconsistency.
AI.conclusion: Class-aware and object-aligned noise modeling significantly improves tracking, but further research is needed to address remaining inconsistency issues in uncertainty estimation.

title: PHASER: Phase-Aware and Semantic Experience Replay for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved remarkable success in language-conditioned robotic manipulation. However, deploying these models in open-ended environments requires continuously acquiring novel skills, a process that inevitably triggers severe catastrophic forgetting of previously learned behaviors. While experience replay (ER) serves as a standard mitigating strategy, naive uniform sampling fundamentally misaligns with the temporal characteristics of manipulation trajectories. It systematically under-samples brief but causally critical sub-skills, leading to phase starvation, and completely overlooks the varying degrees of forgetting across historical tasks. To overcome these limitations, we introduce PHASER, an architecture-agnostic continual learning framework. PHASER employs a phase-centric capacity allocation to guarantee equal memory support for all sub-skills, coupled with a multi-modal interference routing strategy that dynamically prioritizes historical phases at high risk of forgetting. Furthermore, to enable fully autonomous lifelong adaptation, we integrate Auto-PC, a lightweight pipeline combining unsupervised action-signal change-point detection with VLM-based semantic verification to extract temporal boundaries without intensive manual supervision. Evaluated across three VLA backbones on LIBERO continual learning suites, PHASER yields substantial empirical improvements, increasing Average Success Rate (ASR) by up to 31% over matched-budget ER and achieving an 87.8% final ASR on the LIBERO-Goal CL setting.

AI.tldr: PHASER is an architecture-agnostic continual learning framework for VLA models that addresses catastrophic forgetting in robotic manipulation through phase-centric memory allocation, multi-modal interference routing, and an automated pipeline (Auto-PC) for unsupervised temporal boundary extraction, achieving up to 31% improvement in Average Success Rate over standard experience replay on LIBERO benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models deployed in open-ended environments must continuously acquire novel skills, which causes severe catastrophic forgetting of previously learned behaviors. Standard experience replay with uniform sampling is inadequate because it under-samples brief but causally critical sub-skills (phase starvation) and ignores varying degrees of forgetting across historical tasks.
AI.method: PHASER introduces two core mechanisms: (1) phase-centric capacity allocation that guarantees equal memory support for all sub-skills regardless of duration, and (2) multi-modal interference routing that dynamically prioritizes historical phases at high risk of forgetting. Additionally, Auto-PC integrates unsupervised action-signal change-point detection with VLM-based semantic verification to automatically extract temporal boundaries without intensive manual supervision, enabling fully autonomous lifelong adaptation.
AI.result: Evaluated across three VLA backbones on the LIBERO continual learning suite, PHASER increases Average Success Rate (ASR) by up to 31% over matched-budget experience replay baselines and achieves an 87.8% final ASR on the LIBERO-Goal CL setting.
AI.conclusion: PHASER effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting in continual learning for VLA-based robotic manipulation by aligning replay sampling with the temporal structure of manipulation trajectories and task-specific forgetting risk, while Auto-PC removes the need for manual temporal annotation, making the framework practical for autonomous lifelong learning.

title: A 3D Isovist World Model -- Revealing a City's Unseen Geometry and Its Emergent Cross-City Signature
summary: Embodied agents that navigate cities rely on world models that predict how their surroundings will change as they move. But for navigation, what matters is not what the buildings look like; it is where the agent can go. Most world models nonetheless predict appearance, learning how a scene looks rather than the space an agent can move through. Those that do target geometry, such as bird's-eye-view occupancy grids, flatten the three-dimensional environment onto a ground plane, discarding the above-ground and multi-level structure that shapes real navigation. What is missing is a predictive target that captures the navigable geometry an agent actually traverses, without photometric entanglement and without collapsing the third dimension. Our key idea is to model the open volume between buildings, the negative space, encoded as a 3D isovist: a spherical visibility-depth map recording the distance to the nearest surface in every direction. We introduce an embodied world model that predicts the next isovist from a short history of past isovists and a movement action. The prediction is formulated as a depth residual so the decoder inherits sharp building edges, trained with self-rollout scheduled sampling to keep corrupted context on the geometry manifold, and equipped with a persistent latent bird's-eye-view spatial map for cross-path consistency. Our central finding is emergent and unexpected: a single city-blind model trained on Manhattan and Paris develops a cross-city spatial signature, with city identity linearly decodable from its temporal latents far above single-frame baselines, so the signature lives in the learned dynamics rather than in appearance. The representation is lightweight, interpretable, and reproducible, offering a geometric substrate for spatial reasoning in embodied AI, robotics, and urban analysis, released with an open dataset and pipeline.

AI.tldr: An embodied world model predicts 3D isovists (spherical visibility-depth maps) representing navigable space between buildings, capturing geometric structure essential for navigation without photometric entanglement.
AI.motivation: Existing world models predict appearance or flatten 3D environments to 2D, losing crucial navigable geometry information. For navigation, what matters is where an agent can go, not what buildings look like, requiring a predictive target that captures the open volume between buildings without collapsing the third dimension.
AI.method: Models open volume as 3D isovists (spherical visibility-depth maps) predicting next isovist from past isovists and movement actions. Uses depth residual formulation, self-rollout scheduled sampling for geometry manifold training, and persistent latent bird's-eye-view spatial map for cross-path consistency.
AI.result: A single city-blind model trained on Manhattan and Paris develops a cross-city spatial signature linearly decodable from temporal latents. The city identity signature exists in learned dynamics rather than appearance, with lightweight, interpretable geometric representation.
AI.conclusion: This approach provides a geometric substrate for spatial reasoning in embodied AI, robotics, and urban analysis. The representation is lightweight, interpretable, and reproducible, released with an open dataset and pipeline.

title: GN0: Toward a Unified Paradigm for Generation, Evaluation, and Policy Learning in Visual-Language Navigation
summary: Embodied navigation connects intelligent agents with the physical world and is fundamental for general robotic intelligence. Limited availability and quality of navigation data have constrained Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) systems' generalization and long-horizon capabilities. To address this, we curate diverse 3D scenes and develop an automated pipeline for large-scale navigation data, resulting in the GN-Matrix dataset. Building on a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) engine, we introduce a high-fidelity simulation platform supporting interactive roaming and collision-aware navigation. We further propose GN-Bench, the first BEV-based benchmark incorporating dynamic 3DGS avatars for human-robot interaction evaluation. To leverage the simulator, we develop an RL-driven navigation foundation model, Break and Establish (BAE). After supervised learning, DAgger exposes the model to rollout-induced states, breaking narrow expert-centric distributions and enabling downstream RL exploration. This unified VLN paradigm integrates map-based and map-free tasks, including instruction following, human following, and goal navigation. GN-BAE formalizes high-fidelity 3DGS-rendered Bird's Eye View representations as compact memory, unlocking latent spatial reasoning in VLMs. Extensive evaluations on GN-Bench and VLN-CE show that GN0 outperforms state-of-the-art VLN methods. Overall, GN-Matrix offers a unified framework spanning data, simulation, and learning, advancing embodied navigation in research and industrial applications.

AI.tldr: This paper presents GN-Matrix, a unified framework for embodied Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) comprising a large-scale navigation dataset, a high-fidelity 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) simulation platform, a BEV-based benchmark (GN-Bench) for human-robot interaction, and an RL-driven navigation foundation model (GN-BAE/Break and Establish) that achieves state-of-the-art performance on VLN tasks.
AI.motivation: Embodied navigation is fundamental for general robotic intelligence, but Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) systems suffer from limited generalization and long-horizon capabilities due to the scarcity and low quality of available navigation data. A unified framework spanning data generation, simulation, and learning is needed to advance the field.
AI.method: The authors (1) curate diverse 3D scenes and build an automated pipeline for large-scale navigation data, producing the GN-Matrix dataset; (2) develop a high-fidelity simulation platform based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) supporting interactive roaming and collision-aware navigation; (3) propose GN-Bench, the first BEV-based benchmark with dynamic 3DGS avatars for human-robot interaction evaluation; and (4) develop GN-BAE (Break and Establish), an RL-driven navigation foundation model that uses supervised learning followed by DAgger to expose the model to rollout-induced states, breaking narrow expert-centric distributions. The model formalizes 3DGS-rendered Bird's Eye View representations as compact memory and unifies map-based and map-free tasks including instruction following, human following, and goal navigation.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations on GN-Bench and VLN-CE demonstrate that GN0 (the proposed model) outperforms state-of-the-art VLN methods. The BEV-based compact memory representation unlocks latent spatial reasoning in VLMs, and the DAgger-RL paradigm successfully broadens the expert-centric distribution for improved exploration.
AI.conclusion: GN-Matrix provides a comprehensive, unified framework spanning data, simulation, and learning for embodied navigation. It advances both research and industrial applications by addressing the data bottleneck, enabling high-fidelity simulation with human-robot interaction, and delivering a strong navigation foundation model that sets new state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks.

title: Face versus Body Tracking for Human-Robot Interaction: An Egocentric Dataset
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Accepted to the 35th IEEE International Conference on Robot and Human Interactive Communication (RO-MAN 2026)
summary: To enable meaningful human-robot interaction (HRI), a robot must continuously assess engagement by consistently tracking users over time. State-of-the-art computer vision models, however, are heavily optimized for surveillance or autonomous driving. A social robot faces distinct egocentric challenges, such as humans bouncing, obstructing each other, or leaving the frame. Frequent identity switches (IDSW) cause the robot to lose its footing mid-conversation. To address this, we introduce a novel, custom-annotated egocentric dataset collected via the Furhat robot to capture complex social dynamics. We present a systematic evaluation isolating detection errors from tracking logic, comparing face versus body tracking, and assessing the impact of extended spatial memory and appearance re-identification (ReID). Results indicate that increasing spatial memory mitigates prolonged occlusions but fails on complex dynamic events. Integrating ReID resolves complex switches but exhibits opposing effects: it substantially improves body tracking stability, yet causes facial IDSW to spike due to profile angle sensitivity. Ultimately, our optimized pipeline reduces IDSW by 49\%, mitigating interaction breakdowns. Because standard benchmarks lack dense, close-quarter occlusions, this work highlights the critical need for natively captured social dynamics to truly validate HRI perception models.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a custom-annotated egocentric dataset collected via the Furhat robot and evaluates face versus body tracking approaches for social robots, finding that an optimized pipeline can reduce identity switches by 49% while highlighting the need for natively captured social dynamics in HRI benchmarks.
