AI.motivation: Social robots require continuous engagement assessment through user tracking, but state-of-the-art computer vision models optimized for surveillance/autonomous driving fail to handle unique egocentric challenges such as human bouncing, mutual occlusions, and users leaving the frame. Frequent identity switches (IDSW) cause interaction breakdowns in human-robot interaction.
AI.method: Researchers collected a novel, custom-annotated egocentric dataset using the Furhat robot to capture complex social dynamics. They conducted a systematic evaluation isolating detection errors from tracking logic, comparing face versus body tracking approaches, and assessing the impact of extended spatial memory and appearance re-identification (ReID).
AI.result: Increasing spatial memory mitigates prolonged occlusions but fails on complex dynamic events. Integrating ReID improves body tracking stability but causes facial IDSW to spike due to profile angle sensitivity. The optimized pipeline reduces IDSW by 49%, effectively mitigating interaction breakdowns.
AI.conclusion: Standard benchmarks lack dense, close-quarter occlusions, so this work demonstrates the critical need for natively captured social dynamics datasets to truly validate HRI perception models, showing that a well-tuned pipeline can significantly reduce identity switches and maintain interaction continuity.

title: Neural Navigation Functions for Zero-Shot Generalizable Motion Planning
summary: We introduce Neural Navigation Functions (Neural-NF), a learned reactive navigation function capable of zero-shot transfer across unseen environment geometries. Neural-NF places data-driven adaptation within a structured elliptic planner, where the navigation objective is learned while planner structure is preserved by construction. Specifically, intrinsic Laplacian-derived features are mapped to local PDE coefficients, and solving the resulting boundary value problem produces a globally consistent value function on each target domain. For every admissible learned model, the resulting policy is collision-free, provides monotonic descent and a global minimum at the goal by construction. This admits a linearly-solvable optimal-control interpretation for any parameter setting. Empirically, Neural-NF achieves strong zero-shot transfer across diverse geometries and outperforms learned planners that directly predict the value function by up to a $5\times$ improvement.

AI.tldr: Neural Navigation Functions (Neural-NF) is a learned reactive navigation method that achieves zero-shot transfer across unseen environment geometries by embedding data-driven learning within a structured elliptic planner, guaranteeing collision-free policies with monotonic descent by construction.
AI.motivation: Existing learned planners that directly predict value functions often lack generalization to unseen environments and fail to provide safety guarantees such as collision-freedom and convergence. The authors aim to combine the strengths of structured classical planning (e.g., elliptic PDE-based navigation functions with provable properties) with the adaptability of data-driven learning to achieve robust zero-shot transfer.
AI.method: Neural-NF maps intrinsic Laplacian-derived features of the environment to local PDE coefficients via a learned model. Solving the resulting boundary value problem produces a globally consistent navigation value function on each target domain. The planner structure is preserved by construction: the navigation objective is learned while elliptic PDE structure is maintained, ensuring collision-free policies, monotonic descent, and a global minimum at the goal for any admissible learned model. The formulation admits a linearly-solvable optimal-control interpretation.
AI.result: Neural-NF achieves strong zero-shot transfer across diverse and unseen environment geometries. It outperforms learned planners that directly predict the value function by up to 5× improvement in performance.
AI.conclusion: By embedding learning within a structured elliptic PDE framework rather than directly regressing value functions, Neural-NF combines data-driven flexibility with provable navigation guarantees, enabling superior generalization and safety in reactive navigation across novel geometries.

title: Revisiting Embodied Chain-of-Thought for Generalizable Robot Manipulation
summary: Embodied chain-of-thought (CoT) aims to bridge linguistic reasoning and robotic control, but its effective form and integration strategy remain underexplored. In this paper, we revisit embodied CoT for vision-language-action (VLA) models at large scale. We construct the largest embodied CoT corpus to date, comprising 978,743 trajectories, 226.3M samples, and 2592.5 hours of robot data. Through extensive experiments, we find that effective embodied CoT should ground high-level semantic understanding into concrete action guidance, such as end-effector movement descriptions and image-space trajectories, while high-level reasoning alone brings only marginal gains. We further show that explicit CoT does not scale reliably when used as an autoregressive action prefix, as it suffers from compounding inference errors and unstable reasoning-action coupling. To address these limitations, we propose ERVLA, a VLA model that uses embodied CoT as representation-shaping supervision rather than mandatory test-time reasoning. ERVLA is trained with a reasoning-dropout strategy, enabling the model to absorb rich reasoning traces during training while predicting actions directly without CoT decoding during inference. This design improves scalability with increasing pre-training data and avoids autoregressive instability. ERVLA achieves state-of-the-art performance on LIBERO-Plus with an 86.9% success rate and reaches 53.2% success rate on VLABench, demonstrating strong out-of-distribution generalization. In real-robot experiments, ERVLA further outperforms competitive state-of-the-art baselines, especially on tasks requiring semantic disambiguation and long-horizon execution. Code, data, and model checkpoints will be released.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ERVLA, a vision-language-action model that uses embodied chain-of-thought as representation-shaping supervision rather than mandatory test-time reasoning, achieving state-of-the-art performance on LIBERO-Plus (86.9% success rate) and VLABench (53.2% success rate).
AI.motivation: Embodied chain-of-thought (CoT) aims to bridge linguistic reasoning and robotic control, but its effective form and integration strategy remain underexplored. The authors found that high-level reasoning alone brings only marginal gains, and explicit CoT used as an autoregressive action prefix suffers from compounding inference errors and unstable reasoning-action coupling.
AI.method: The authors constructed the largest embodied CoT corpus to date (978,743 trajectories, 226.3M samples, 2592.5 hours of robot data) and proposed ERVLA, a VLA model that uses embodied CoT as representation-shaping supervision rather than mandatory test-time reasoning. ERVLA is trained with a reasoning-dropout strategy, enabling the model to absorb rich reasoning traces during training while predicting actions directly without CoT decoding during inference.
AI.result: ERVLA achieves state-of-the-art performance on LIBERO-Plus with an 86.9% success rate and reaches 53.2% success rate on VLABench, demonstrating strong out-of-distribution generalization. In real-robot experiments, ERVLA outperforms competitive state-of-the-art baselines, especially on tasks requiring semantic disambiguation and long-horizon execution.
AI.conclusion: Effective embodied CoT should ground high-level semantic understanding into concrete action guidance (such as end-effector movement descriptions and image-space trajectories). Explicit CoT does not scale reliably when used as an autoregressive action prefix due to compounding inference errors and unstable reasoning-action coupling. By using CoT as representation-shaping supervision with a reasoning-dropout strategy, ERVLA improves scalability and avoids autoregressive instability while achieving superior performance.

title: Worth Remembering: Surprise-Gated Robot Episodic Memory
summary: Robots solving generalist tasks need to be able to ground instructions in their past experience, since humans may refer to notable past events when giving a task (e.g., ``Take me to where the chemical spill happened yesterday''). Since memory limits make storing all past events infeasible, long-term robot memory must be selective, ideally retaining only those episodes with high utility for future tasks. However, future tasks are not typically given a priori for generalist robots. To select generically useful memories, we propose Bayesian surprise as a gating mechanism for memory formation. We present an approach to compute surprise in a semantically rich deployment-agnostic latent space provided by V-JEPA-2. Using our gated episodic memory to augment 4D scene graph-based spatial memory, we show a consistent improvement over state-of-the-art benchmarks in robot question answering, outperforming prior robot memory methods by $\geq12\%$ for temporal, spatial, and binary questions, and surpassing the performance of supervised and non-causal methods with an unsupervised causal method in event segmentation tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Bayesian surprise as a gating mechanism for selective long-term episodic memory formation in robots, using V-JEPA-2's latent space, and demonstrates consistent improvements in robot question answering and event segmentation over state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: Generalist robots need to ground instructions in past experience, but storing all past events is infeasible due to memory limits. Since future tasks are unknown a priori, robots need a way to selectively retain only generally useful memories for future tasks.
AI.method: The authors propose Bayesian surprise as an unsupervised gating mechanism for episodic memory formation. Surprise is computed in a deployment-agnostic, semantically rich latent space derived from V-JEPA-2. The gated episodic memory augments 4D scene graph-based spatial memory for robot reasoning.
AI.result: The approach consistently improves over state-of-the-art benchmarks in robot question answering, outperforming prior robot memory methods by ≥12% on temporal, spatial, and binary questions. It also surpasses supervised and non-causal methods on event segmentation tasks using an unsupervised causal approach.
AI.conclusion: Bayesian surprise in a V-JEPA-2 latent space is an effective, unsupervised, and deployment-agnostic criterion for selective episodic memory formation, enabling robots to retain generically useful memories that improve performance on downstream tasks such as question answering and event segmentation.

title: Optimal Design and Analytical Modeling of a Soft Fin-Ray Effect Gripper Finger Using the Finite Rigid Elements Method
summary: Fin Ray-inspired soft grippers offer a promising solution for gently handling delicate, irregular objects, especially in agriculture. The objective of this research is to design, fabricate, and model a Fin Ray Effect (FRE) soft gripper finger to enable precise force control in future applications. This design aims to gently grasp delicate agricultural products, such as tomatoes, that require both adaptability and accurate force application. To address the inherent challenges of soft robotics, including nonlinear behavior, infinite degrees of freedom, and variable material properties, the Finite Rigid Elements Method (FREM) was employed for modeling. This method preserves analytical accuracy while providing a reliable foundation for the development of a force controller in later stages. A detailed Finite Element Model (FEM) was created using ANSYS, and the analytical results were validated through simulation and experimental testing. The gripper's fingers were optimized based on four key criteria: tip displacement, total deflection, stress distribution, and contact force. The optimal finger configuration includes a length of 30 mm, rib spacing of 10 mm, seven ribs angled at -15 deg, and a rib thickness of 1 mm. Theoretical modeling using the FREM predicted finger deformation with a 3% error, while the ANSYS numerical model achieved 2% error.

AI.tldr: This paper designs, fabricates, and models a Fin Ray Effect (FRE) soft gripper finger for gentle grasping of delicate agricultural products, using the Finite Rigid Elements Method (FREM) for analytical modeling validated by ANSYS FEM simulations and experiments, achieving deformation prediction errors as low as 2–3%.
AI.motivation: Delicate and irregular agricultural products (e.g., tomatoes) require grippers that combine adaptability with precise force control. However, soft robotics inherently suffer from nonlinear behavior, infinite degrees of freedom, and variable material properties, making accurate modeling and force control challenging. A reliable analytical model is needed as a foundation for future force controller development.
AI.method: A Fin Ray-inspired soft gripper finger was designed and fabricated. The Finite Rigid Elements Method (FREM) was employed for analytical modeling to capture the finger's mechanical behavior. A detailed Finite Element Model (FEM) was built in ANSYS for numerical simulation. The finger geometry was optimized across four criteria: tip displacement, total deflection, stress distribution, and contact force. Analytical results were validated against both simulation and experimental testing.
AI.result: The optimal gripper finger configuration was determined: 30 mm length, 10 mm rib spacing, seven ribs at −15°, and 1 mm rib thickness. The FREM analytical model predicted finger deformation with approximately 3% error, while the ANSYS numerical model achieved approximately 2% error, demonstrating high modeling accuracy and reliability.
AI.conclusion: The FREM-based analytical model provides a computationally efficient yet accurate framework for modeling Fin Ray soft gripper fingers, closely matching FEM and experimental results. This validated model establishes a solid foundation for developing precise force controllers for gentle grasping of delicate agricultural products.

title: Let the Dynamics Flow: Stable Flow Matching Dynamical Systems
summary: Flow matching has recently emerged as a powerful approach for imitation learning, enabling scalable, expressive, and multimodal motion policies. However, incorporating formal stability guarantees into these generative models, a prerequisite to ensure safe and generalizable robot behaviors, remains a significant challenge. While modeling robot motions as dynamical systems allows for such stability-based inductive biases, existing frameworks struggle to capture the rich action distributions inherent in complex robotic tasks. This paper introduces Stable Flow Matching Dynamical Systems (SFMDS), a novel framework that bridges the gap between high-capacity generative modeling and formal Lyapunov stability guarantees. SFMDS parametrizes dynamical systems via flow matching while simultaneously constraining the model to a family of stable solutions. We propose two variants: a soft constraint based on a penalty term, and a hard structural constraint embedded directly in the model architecture. We further extend both formulations to Lie groups. Experiments on benchmark datasets, in simulation, and on a humanoid robot show that SFMDS learns stable, scalable, and multimodal dynamical systems in low- and high-dimensional state spaces, enabling safe and expressive robot motion generation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Stable Flow Matching Dynamical Systems (SFMDS), a framework that combines flow matching-based generative modeling with formal Lyapunov stability guarantees for robot imitation learning, enabling safe, scalable, and multimodal motion generation.
AI.motivation: Flow matching has become a powerful tool for imitation learning with expressive, multimodal motion policies, but it lacks formal stability guarantees—critical for safe and generalizable robot behavior. Existing dynamical-systems-based approaches offer stability but fail to capture rich, complex action distributions. Bridging high-capacity generative modeling with formal stability remains an open challenge.
AI.method: SFMDS parametrizes dynamical systems via flow matching while constraining the model to a family of Lyapunov-stable solutions. Two variants are proposed: (1) a soft constraint using a penalty term in the training objective, and (2) a hard structural constraint embedded directly into the model architecture. Both formulations are further extended to Lie groups to handle robotic state spaces such as rotations.
AI.result: Experiments on benchmark datasets, simulations, and a real humanoid robot demonstrate that SFMDS learns stable, scalable, and multimodal dynamical systems in both low- and high-dimensional state spaces, successfully producing safe and expressive robot motion generation.
AI.conclusion: SFMDS effectively bridges the gap between expressive generative modeling and formal stability guarantees, providing a principled framework for learning stable, multimodal robot motion policies that are deployable on real robotic platforms.

title: Denoising Tells When to Replan: Denoising-Variance Adaptive Chunking for Flow-Based Robot Policies
summary: Action chunking has become a common inference strategy for flow-based robot policies, improving action coherence by modeling multi-step temporal dependencies in demonstrations. However, the execution horizon is still typically set as an empirical fixed value, overlooking that predictable free-space motions and precision-critical interaction phases often require different replanning frequencies. In this work, we first show that the denoising process of flow-based policies contains an intrinsic signal of task phases: clean-action estimates remain stable during predictable motion phases, but fluctuate more strongly around contact-rich or precision-sensitive operations. Motivated by this observation, we propose DVAC (Denoising-Variance Adaptive Chunking), a test-time method that adaptively determines how many actions to execute from each predicted chunk. DVAC measures the variance of clean-action estimates over the final denoising steps, executes the stable low-variance prefix, and replans before high-variance future actions are committed. To transfer across tasks and rollouts, DVAC further calibrates the threshold with a rolling estimate of the local variance scale. Experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin, CALVIN, and real-world manipulation show that DVAC improves task success while reducing replanning frequency. With a $π_{0.5}$-based policy, DVAC improves LIBERO success from 94.75% to 98.00% and reduces replanning by 43.0%, while also yielding aggregate gains on RoboTwin and CALVIN and improving real-world execution efficiency.

AI.tldr: DVAC (Denoising-Variance Adaptive Chunking) is a test-time method that adaptively determines how many actions to execute from each predicted chunk in flow-based robot policies by leveraging the variance of clean-action estimates during the denoising process, improving task success while reducing replanning frequency.
AI.motivation: Existing flow-based robot policies use action chunking with a fixed execution horizon, ignoring that different task phases (e.g., predictable free-space motions vs. contact-rich or precision-critical interactions) require different replanning frequencies. This mismatch leads to either unnecessary replanning or unsafe action commitment.
AI.method: DVAC exploits the observation that clean-action estimates in flow-based policy denoising remain stable during predictable phases but fluctuate during precision-sensitive operations. It measures the variance of clean-action estimates over the final denoising steps, executes the stable low-variance prefix of the action chunk, and replans before high-variance actions are committed. A rolling estimate of local variance scale is used to calibrate the threshold, enabling cross-task and cross-rollout transfer.
AI.result: DVAC improves task success and reduces replanning frequency across LIBERO, RoboTwin, CALVIN, and real-world manipulation benchmarks. With a π₀.₅-based policy, LIBERO success improves from 94.75% to 98.00% with a 43.0% reduction in replanning. Aggregate gains are also observed on RoboTwin and CALVIN, along with improved real-world execution efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The denoising process of flow-based policies provides an intrinsic signal for adaptive action chunking. By using denoising variance to modulate the execution horizon at test time, DVAC achieves both higher success rates and greater computational efficiency without requiring task-specific tuning, demonstrating broad applicability across simulation and real-world manipulation tasks.

title: Semantic-weighted ICP for LiDAR Odometry: Class-Aware Residual Reweighting for Robust Scan Registration
summary: LiDAR odometry is a fundamental component of autonomous robotic systems, relying on geometric registration between consecutive point clouds to estimate ego-motion. However, traditional geometric approaches often degrade in dynamic or unstructured environments due to unreliable correspondences caused by moving objects, sparse geometric features, vegetation, and semantically ambiguous structures. Existing works have shown that, some of these limitations can be addressed by introducing semantic information from the environment in the registration process. In this work, we build on this, and show that not all elements in the environment are equally relevant for registration. Hence, we propose a semantic class-weighted ICP for LiDAR odometry. Instead of strictly filtering out points belonging to specific semantic classes, the proposed approach weights the residuals of points belonging to semantic categories based on their expected geometric stability. This strategy enables informative but potentially unstable structures, to contribute to the registration process while mitigating the influence of dynamic objects. The experimental evaluation was conducted on the SemanticKITTI and RELLIS-3D datasets, which include urban, highway, rural, and off-road environments. The empirical results show that the proposed Semantic-weighted ICP improves pose estimation, especially in challenging off-road scenarios where conventional rigid features are scarce. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that the effectiveness of this weighting strategy is highly environment-dependent, influenced by the structural and semantic composition of the scene.

AI.tldr: A semantic class-weighted ICP method for LiDAR odometry is proposed, where residuals of points from different semantic categories are weighted by their expected geometric stability, improving pose estimation especially in challenging off-road environments.
AI.motivation: Traditional geometric LiDAR odometry approaches degrade in dynamic or unstructured environments due to unreliable correspondences caused by moving objects, sparse geometric features, vegetation, and semantically ambiguous structures. Existing semantic-aided methods exist, but they do not account for the fact that not all environmental elements are equally relevant for registration.
AI.method: A semantic class-weighted ICP (Iterative Closest Point) algorithm for LiDAR odometry. Rather than rigidly filtering out specific semantic classes, the method assigns weights to residuals of points based on the expected geometric stability of their semantic category. This allows potentially unstable but informative structures to contribute to registration while reducing the influence of dynamic objects.
AI.result: Evaluated on SemanticKITTI and RELLIS-3D datasets across urban, highway, rural, and off-road environments. The proposed semantic-weighted ICP improves pose estimation, particularly in challenging off-road scenarios where conventional rigid features are scarce. The analysis also shows that the effectiveness of the weighting strategy is highly environment-dependent, influenced by the structural and semantic composition of the scene.
AI.conclusion: Weighting semantic classes by their geometric stability in the ICP registration process is a more flexible and effective strategy than hard filtering, yielding improved LiDAR odometry performance. The approach is especially beneficial in unstructured off-road environments, though its effectiveness varies with scene composition, suggesting that adaptive, environment-aware weighting strategies may be a promising future direction.

title: Multi-Robot Bearing-only Pose Estimation via Angle Rigidity
summary: This letter proposes a novel distributed bearing-based pose estimator for time-varying multi-robot systems. The method uses angles computed from body-frame bearings to estimate the robots' positions in $\mathbb{R}^3$ without knowledge of their orientations. The orientations in $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ are recovered from the estimated positions, the bearings, and the bearing derivatives. The proposed observer only requires the (directed) sensing topology to be \textit{angle-rigid}, a weaker condition than the commonly used ones like bearing rigidity. Local uniform exponential stability of the proposed observer is established under the assumption of persistently exciting motions for a subset of robots. Simulations are presented and discussed to evaluate the scheme's effectiveness and practicality.

AI.tldr: This letter proposes a distributed bearing-based pose estimator for time-varying multi-robot systems that estimates robot positions in ℝ³ without orientation knowledge, using angle-rigidity as a weaker condition than bearing rigidity, with local uniform exponential stability under persistently exciting motions.
AI.motivation: Existing bearing-based pose estimation methods typically require stronger topological conditions like bearing rigidity. There is a need for a more flexible approach that can work with weaker topology requirements and handle time-varying multi-robot systems where orientation knowledge is not available.
AI.method: The method computes angles from body-frame bearings to estimate robot positions in ℝ³ without orientation knowledge. Orientations in SO(3) are recovered from estimated positions, bearings, and their derivatives. The observer only requires the directed sensing topology to be angle-rigid, which is weaker than bearing rigidity.
AI.result: Local uniform exponential stability of the proposed observer is established under the assumption of persistently exciting motions for a subset of robots. Simulations demonstrate the scheme's effectiveness and practicality.
AI.conclusion: The proposed angle-rigidity-based approach provides a more flexible and weaker topological condition than traditional bearing rigidity, enabling distributed pose estimation in time-varying multi-robot systems without requiring full orientation knowledge.

title: PointAction: 3D Points as Universal Action Representations for Robot Control
summary: Video-Action Models (VAMs) leverage the broad visual dynamics captured by pre-trained video diffusion models, offering a promising path toward generalizable robot manipulation. However, RGB-only video rollouts are not directly actionable: they leave metric 3D motion, contact geometry, and fine-grained spatial constraints under-specified, making action grounding ambiguous. Meanwhile, scaling action supervision across diverse tasks and embodiments remains costly. We present PointAction, a framework that bridges video predictions to robot actions through explicit point-based 4D modeling. PointAction fine-tunes a foundation video generation model to jointly predict future RGB frames and dynamic 3D pointmaps, producing temporally consistent 3D motion of task-relevant scene geometry. These point dynamics serve as a structured, embodiment-agnostic action interface, which a diffusion-based action decoder maps to executable robot actions. By using metric 3D point dynamics as the interface between video prediction and control, PointAction reduces the ambiguity of RGB-only action grounding and supports transfer across tasks and embodiments with limited action supervision. Experiments show that PointAction achieves state-of-the-art 4D generation quality on robot scenes, outperforms existing baselines in simulation, and generalizes to two real robot arms unseen during pretraining.

AI.tldr: PointAction bridges video prediction and robot control via point-based 4D modeling, jointly generating RGB frames and dynamic 3D pointmaps to reduce action grounding ambiguity and enable cross-task, cross-embodiment generalization with limited action supervision.
AI.motivation: Video-Action Models (VAMs) built on pre-trained video diffusion models are promising for generalizable robot manipulation, but RGB-only rollouts leave metric 3D motion, contact geometry, and fine-grained spatial constraints under-specified, making action grounding ambiguous. Additionally, scaling action supervision across diverse tasks and embodiments remains costly.
AI.method: PointAction fine-tunes a foundation video generation model to jointly predict future RGB frames and dynamic 3D pointmaps, yielding temporally consistent 3D motion of task-relevant scene geometry. These 4D point dynamics serve as a structured, embodiment-agnostic action interface, which a diffusion-based action decoder maps to executable robot actions.
AI.result: PointAction achieves state-of-the-art 4D generation quality on robot scenes, outperforms existing baselines in simulation, and generalizes to two real robot arms unseen during pretraining.
AI.conclusion: Using metric 3D point dynamics as the interface between video prediction and control effectively reduces the ambiguity of RGB-only action grounding and supports transfer across tasks and embodiments with limited action supervision, establishing point-based 4D modeling as a practical bridge between generative video models and robot manipulation.

title: Preference-Calibrated Human-in-the-Loop Reinforcement Learning for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning (HIL-RL) improves sample efficiency in real-robot manipulation through online human intervention. However, successful trajectories may include suboptimal actions that deviate from the desired task-execution path and force human intervention. Existing HIL-RL methods typically apply the consistent credit assignment principle to all transitions, uniformly propagating discounted terminal rewards through suboptimal segments, ignoring the actual contribution of each transition to task success. This overestimates Q-values for critic learning and indirectly misguides actor updates toward suboptimal behavior patterns. To this end, we propose PACT, a Preference-calibrated Actor-Critic Training framework that leverages the implicit preference signals induced by intervention to perform credit reassignment on identified suboptimal segments while directly guiding policy training for unbiased critic-actor learning. Specifically, we first design a progress model that learns from human demonstration and identifies suboptimal segments for credit correction. Then, from the human action and resampled policy action at the intervention state, we build preference pairs to define a counterfactual advantage that penalizes Bellman targets of the identified suboptimal segment, enabling directional credit calibration. Moreover, we directly align the policy with human corrective actions in the bounded mean space, providing an additional signal beyond critic-guided updates. Across five real-robot manipulation tasks, PACT improves the average success rate by 24.5% and achieves 1.3 times faster convergence, thereby improving both RL sample efficiency and performance. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/HILRL-A1X-BC05.

AI.tldr: PACT proposes a Preference-calibrated Actor-Critic Training framework that uses human intervention signals to perform credit reassignment on suboptimal segments, improving sample efficiency and success rates in real-robot manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing Human-in-the-loop RL methods uniformly propagate rewards through suboptimal segments, ignoring actual transition contributions and overestimating Q-values, which misguides actor updates toward suboptimal behaviors.
AI.method: PACT employs a progress model to identify suboptimal segments, builds preference pairs from human and policy actions at intervention states to define counterfactual advantage, and directly aligns policies with human corrective actions in bounded mean space.
AI.result: Across five real-robot tasks, PACT improves average success rate by 24.5% and achieves 1.3× faster convergence, demonstrating improved RL sample efficiency and performance.
AI.conclusion: By leveraging implicit preference signals from human intervention for credit reassignment and direct policy alignment, PACT effectively addresses the overestimation problem in HIL-RL, enabling more accurate critic learning and better actor updates.

title: Self-Refining Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Vision-Conditioned UAV Navigation
summary: Deep reinforcement learning has shown strong potential for enabling autonomous robots to learn complex navigational tasks. However, its practical use still depends heavily on human designed reward functions and repeated manual fine tuning, which is time consuming and does not guarantee high success in the desired task. This paper presents AgenticRL, agent guided reinforcement learning framework that increases autonomy in reward design, policy refinement, and real world deployment for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV) navigation tasks. AgenticRL uses a multimodal generative pre-trained tansformer (GPT) agent to interpret task information and visual scene observations, generate task specific reward functions, train policies using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm, and then act as a critic by evaluating the trained policy through diagnosis packets to generate feedback. Based on this feedback, the agent identifies failure modes and refines the reward function in a closed loop self improvement process. To further leverage the multimodal GPT agent during inference, AgenticRL uses real world images and natural language task information to automatically identify the active scenario and select the appropriate trained policy for execution. The framework is evaluated on multiple navigational tasks, including gate traversal, obstacle avoidance, wall barrier crossing with landing, trajectory following, and motion behavior learning. Experimental results show that the closed loop refinement process improves policy behavior compared with initial rewards by 71%. We also demonstrate sim-to-real transfer of the proposed framework, achieving a real world success rate of 91% and a sim-to-real accuracy of 94%.

AI.tldr: AgenticRL is an agent-guided reinforcement learning framework that uses a multimodal GPT agent to autonomously design reward functions, refine policies, and deploy them for UAV navigation, achieving 71% improvement through closed-loop refinement, 91% real-world success rate, and 94% sim-to-real accuracy.
AI.motivation: Deep reinforcement learning for autonomous robot navigation relies heavily on human-designed reward functions and repeated manual fine-tuning, which is time-consuming and does not guarantee high task success. There is a need for greater autonomy in reward design, policy refinement, and real-world deployment, particularly for UAV navigation tasks.
AI.method: AgenticRL employs a multimodal GPT agent that interprets task information and visual scene observations to generate task-specific reward functions. Policies are trained using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). The agent then evaluates trained policies via diagnosis packets, identifies failure modes, and refines the reward function in a closed-loop self-improvement process. During inference, the multimodal GPT agent uses real-world images and natural language to identify the active scenario and select the appropriate trained policy for execution.
AI.result: Evaluated on multiple UAV navigation tasks (gate traversal, obstacle avoidance, wall barrier crossing with landing, trajectory following, and motion behavior learning). The closed-loop refinement process improved policy behavior by 71% compared to initial rewards. Sim-to-real transfer achieved a 91% real-world success rate and 94% sim-to-real accuracy.
AI.conclusion: AgenticRL demonstrates that a multimodal GPT agent can effectively automate reward design, policy refinement, and scenario-aware policy selection for UAV navigation. The framework significantly reduces human intervention while achieving high performance and robust sim-to-real transfer across diverse navigational tasks.

title: Humanoid-GPT: Scaling Data and Structure for Zero-Shot Motion Tracking
summary: We introduce Humanoid-GPT, a GPT-style Transformer with causal attention trained on a billion-scale motion corpus for whole-body control. Unlike prior shallow MLP trackers constrained by scarce data and an agility-generalization trade-off, Humanoid-GPT is pre-trained on a 2B-frame retargeted corpus that unifies all major mocap datasets with large-scale in-house recordings. Scaling both data and model capacity yields a single generative Transformer that tracks highly dynamic behaviors while achieving unprecedented zero-shot generalization to unseen motions and control tasks. Extensive experiments and scaling analyses show that our model establishes a new performance frontier, demonstrating robust zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks while simultaneously tracking highly dynamic and complex motions.

AI.tldr: Humanoid-GPT is a GPT-style causal attention Transformer for whole-body control, pre-trained on 2B frames from unified mocap datasets, achieving unprecedented zero-shot generalization to unseen motions and tasks while maintaining high-fidelity dynamic tracking.
AI.motivation: Prior shallow MLP trackers were constrained by scarce training data and a fundamental agility-generalization trade-off, limiting their ability to simultaneously capture highly dynamic behaviors and generalize to unseen scenarios.
AI.method: A causal attention Transformer architecture trained on a 2B-frame retargeted corpus that unifies all major motion capture datasets with large-scale in-house recordings, with systematic scaling of both data volume and model capacity to enable single generative model performance.
AI.result: Establishes a new performance frontier demonstrating robust zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks while simultaneously tracking highly dynamic and complex motions, with scaling analyses confirming that increased data and model capacity yield superior performance across diverse behaviors.
AI.conclusion: Single generative Transformer models can simultaneously achieve high-fidelity motion tracking and broad zero-shot generalization capabilities when trained on massive, unified motion corpora, overcoming the agility-generalization trade-off that limited prior shallow trackers.
